speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday last the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) drew attention to an order of the house which had been passed on March 22, with respect to certain correspondence and documents. Replying to the motion I intimated that should a reexamination of the file disclose material which could be tabled without contravening established practice, I would have it brought down.
Constitutional practice as followed by successive governments maintains that documents pertaining to clemency or the royal prerogative of mercy should be treated as confidential, and that it would not be proper or advisable to make them public. In this case I find that the record contains only papers relating to an application for clemency. I also find that there appears to be nothing in this instance which would warrant an exception to the practice to which I have referred.
I therefore can only reply to my hon. friend that in this case there are on record no papers which can be produced in keeping with the established practice recognized by parliament.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO

speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee of supply.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, with respect to the
proceedings of parliament with relation to the ro.yal visit, obviously there are three courses, any one of which may be followed. The first would be that the house and parliament should continue in session during the period that their majesties may be in Canada provided that we have not concluded our business by that time. The second course would be that parliament should adjourn over the period of their majesties' visit if we have not then concluded our business, and the third course would be that parliament should be prorogued at the time his majesty may be in the city, assuming that parliament has by that time concluded its business.
With respect to the first course, namely that of having parliament continue in session while their majesties are in Canada, I have noticed there has been some comment and suggestion in a section of the press to the effect that hon. members would perhaps be best showing their real appreciation of the duties owing the sovereign were parliament to continue in session while their majesties are in Canada. There have been other views expressed. I wish to state quite frankly to the house my own views in regard to that particular suggestion.
In the first place I perhaps should point out that in 1935 at the time of the silver jubilee of the late King George V, this house was adjourned over the period of the jubilee to permit the Prime Minister of the day to attend the ceremonies in London. If I recollect aright my colleague the Right Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and myself rather
took exception to that adjournment. It might therefore be thought we were arguing against ourselves if we do not to-day support the idea of the house continuing in session during the period of their majesties' visit. I should like to point out that the parallel is not as close as it might appear to be, inasmuch as in 1935 the prime minister of the day, through illness, unfortunately had not been able to be in the house during the two preceding months and the business had been carried on throughout that period by an acting prime minister. Moreover, in attending the jubilee the prime minister alone was going to England; it did not involve what might be the wishes of his colleagues or of the members of the house generally. The situation at this time is, I think, quite different in that respect. Their majesties will be coming to Canada, and without a doubt all members of the house will wish to consider how best they may meet the wishes of their constituents and tender such measure of respect as they will wish to do to the sovereign and his royal consort when their majesties are in this country. I am inclined to think that the general feeling throughout the country will be that while their majesties are in Canada it would be fortunate for all concerned if we could have a truce to party strife both within the walls of parliament and pretty much throughout the country. I hope it will not be thought that in saying this I am trying in any way to save the government from criticism. I do not expect to be able to do that by anything which may be said at any time. But I do point out what I think will be the wishes of the country generally with respect to acute political discussions during the course of the royal visit.
I might mention another factor which I believe is important. It is that the public itself is entitled to be in a position to follow carefully from day to day the proceedings of parliament. I doubt very much, if parliament were in session during the time of the royal visit, with the amount of attention that will be given in the press to the proceedings of the royal visit and matters incidental thereto, whether the business of parliament would be either reported or followed as closely through the press as people generally in the country might wish it to be.
May I mention another matter which has also been referred to in the press, and that is the manner in which the Prime Minister might best discharge his duties while their majesties are here. It has been said in different quarters that my duty as Prime Minister is primarily here in the House of Commons. With that I wholly agree. It is
Royal Visit and Parliament

said by some, however, that I should be carrying on here with parliament in session rather than acting as minister in attendance on the king in the course of his majesty's visit throughout Canada. That is a very natural comment. I wish, however, to put before hon. members the situation precisely as I see it.
There is to be considered the question of courtesy due the crown. That I think is an important matter at all times, perhaps not the all-important one but one of which at least full account should be taken. I recall that when the late King George V and Queen Mary visited Canada as Duke and Duchess of York prior to the time their majesties ascended the throne, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Lady Laurier accompanied the royal couple throughout their visit to the Pacific coast. They did so as an expression of national courtesy to members of the royal family-members of the royal family who it was expected might become in the course of time the king and queen of the United Kingdom and of the other nations of the commonwealth. At present, however, it is not merely members of the royal family who may in the course of time succeed to the throne, it is the actual holder of the crown, the king himself, and the queen, who will be in Canada for the first time. That of itself places a very great responsibility upon the government, and perhaps, I may be permitted to add, upon the Prime Minister in particular with respect to all that pertains to the position of the king while his majesty is in this country. As I say, the visit will be made by the actual holder of the crown, and because of that, this country and this government will have a great and grave responsibility with respect to the position of the sovereign, not only in relation to our own people but in relation also to the peoples of all the other nations of the commonwealth. His Majesty the King will not be accompanied by any member of the ministry of the United Kingdom or by any minister from any other part of the British commonwealth. I therefore feel that in the United Kingdom, as, indeed, in all parts of the empire, there will be naturally a feeling in the minds of those in responsible positions that a very special obligation rests upon the government of this country which his majesty will be visiting at the time to see that his majesty's position in every respect is respected and protected as much as it can possibly be.
I notice it has been said that there seemed to be no necessity why the Prime Minister's car should be attached to the royal train and the Prime Minister accompany the king throughout his tour of Canada. May I say in regard to that, and the kind of thought

which underlies it, that it is a constitutional custom which has been observed for not only years but centuries that the sovereign, when he travels in respect to matters of an official nature, matters of state, should be accompanied by at least one of his constitutional advisers and should not at any time be left without some minister of the crown with whom he may confer on questions which may require the advice of his ministers. It has been suggested, and I must say it is a suggestion which appeals very strongly in many ways to myself, that that service might be performed by different ministers attending, rather than the Prime Minister. I have not the least doubt that his majesty is looking forward to different ministers of the crown being with him as he passes through the different provinces of the dominion. That is, I think, a courtesy and a constitutional responsibility which ought to be observed. But I have had to ask myself the question whether, all circumstances considered, an arrangement of that kind would suffice, in the eyes of the people of Canada and peoples in other parts of the empire, to meet the obligation which will rest upon the government at the time of the royal visit. I rather believe the people of Canada will expect the Prime Minister, simply because he is prime minister, to be the one who will accompany the king in the course of his visit throughout Canada.
But there is another reason which I think I should mention, although it is perhaps unnecessary to stress it. These are very anxious and critical times in the affairs of the world, and his majesty will wish to be informed while in Canada upon matters affecting Canada's external relations as well as those, which affect our internal relations. In other words, his majesty will expect in relation to himself while in Canada fulfilment of exactly the same type of obligation on the part of his Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs that His Excellency the Governor General expects. It is part of my duty as Prime Minister and part of my duty as Secretary of State for External Affairs to discuss from time to time with his excellency matters of great concern to this country in common with other parts of the British Commonwealth of Nations. His excellency expects to be shown the important dispatches that come from day to day to the office of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and it is a part of my duty as Secretary of State for External Affairs to see that these dispatches are communicated to his excellency and that he has an opportunity to discuss with me questions that arise out of them.

Royal Visit and Parliament
In regard to the external affairs of the United Kingdom, foreign affairs as they pertain to the government of the United Kingdom, those, of course, will be carried on in Great Britain in the same manner, while his majesty is in Canada, as they would be carried on were his majesty in Great Britain, with the exception that counsellors of state instead of his majesty will be administering the affairs of the United Kingdom. The counsellors of state will be advised by his majesty's ministers of the crown with respect to foreign affairs of the United Kingdom. So far as Canada is concerned in relation to Canada's external affairs, it will be the duty of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to perform, as I have said, the same duties towards his majesty in Canada as would be performed by his majesty's ministers in the United Kingdom in relation to their affairs or as are being performed at the present time with his excellency in relation to our own affairs.
I need hardly say that it would greatly lessen my duties and responsibilities if some other arrangement could properly be made, but I must say that it would not be meeting either my duties or my responsibilities as I see them myself, and as I believe they would be viewed by the people of Canada generally, if I did not undertake the obligation and the duty, as well as enjoying the honour of accompanying his majesty throughout the whole of his Canadian tour. I wish to present one possibility which I pray may not arise but a possibility for which it is my responsibility to have regard. Having in mind situations as we have seen them arise, even since this parliament assembled-the situation that developed in Czechoslovakia, the situation that developed in Albania, and the state of affairs which we all know exists at the present time

I ask hon. members this question: What would the people of Canada say, were another crisis, either as great as those which I have mentioned, or greater, to arise when his majesty might be on the prairies or in British Columbia and the government had permitted the king to be there at such a time without having the opportunity of conferring with the Prime Minister of the part of his realm which he had come to visit, or with his Secretary of State who, so far as Canada is concerned, is responsible for advising on External Affairs.
These are matters which I have had to consider very carefully in my present position. I have been long enough in public life to know the kind of comment that is likely to arise out of any relations of a Prime Minister with matters that have to do with court etiquette or other questions of the kind, not
to be fully alive to what may be said in party political ways with respect to my not remaining here and being present with other members attending to the business of parliament, instead of being on a royal tour. It is for that reason that I have asked you, Mr. Speaker, this afternoon to permit me to say these words on a motion to go into committee of supply so that every hon. member will have the opportunity, if he so desires, to express himself frankly here and now with respect to what he conceives my duty and obligation to be in relation to his majesty in the course of his visit to Canada.
May I observe that all hon. members in this house are representing their constituencies here. If any hon. member believes that his constituents would think it more the duty of the Prime Minister to have parliament continue in session instead of adjourn its proceedings while their majesties are here and to remain here himself at his post, allowing the king to proceed from one end of Canada to the other during the period of his majesty's stay in Canada, unaccompanied by his Prime Minister or by his Secretary of State for External Affairs, I would ask that hon. member to rise and say so now, and let this house consider the matter as part of its responsibility to the citizens of Canada generally. I can only speak for one constituency, the one I represent, the constituency of Prince Albert.
I believe the people of that constituency would think I had failed in my duty not only to the king but also to the people of Canada were I to take any other course than the one I have suggested as the right and proper one to take in the circumstances I have mentioned.
I have given reasons why I think it would be inadvisable for parliament to continue in session during the short time their majesties are to be here. I now mention the other course, which would be that of an adjournment over the period. I believe I have already anticipated the arguments touching the wisdom of an adjournment. I should like to make it quite clear that if we are obliged to adjourn because the business of parliament is not completed when their majesties arrive in Canada we will adjourn from the Friday evening, preceding the date on which their majesties arrive at Quebec, which would be May 12-their majesties arrive on May 15- and the house will stand adjourned until June 19, which is the first Monday following the date on which their majesties will leave Canada on their return to the old country. I believe it is on Thursday, June 15 that their majesties leave Halifax. For that reason I mention now that it will be on June 19 that the house would resume.
Royal Visit and Parliament

The third course is, of course, the possibility of prorogation by his majesty during his stay in this city. May I make perfectly clear the position of the government with respect to prorogation. I said at the beginning of this session that, desirous as we might be to be through with the business of parliament at the time of their majesties' arrival, the government would put no pressure on the house to expedite its business in any way on that account if expedition meant that the business could not be satisfactorily dealt with in the intervening time. May I make this point clear in the first instance. The government itself did not decide upon the date upon which the visit of their majesties was to take place. We were given the date that suited their majesties, because there are many obligations of which their majesties have to take account, and the time of their arrival in Canada was determined without any advice in the matter of fixing a particular date, except for seeking to have a time selected that would best meet the convenience of the king and queen. But we did call parliament in the second week of January in order that there might be, having regard to other sessions, what we believed would be sufficient time within which to enable the house to conclude its business.
I was very careful, when I spoke to His Excellency the Governor General about the possibility of parliament being prorogued by his majesty, to make it perfectly clear to his excellency that the last thing I would wish to do would be in any way to have it assumed that, through a desire on the part of hon. members to participate in a prorogation ceremony at which his majesty would be present,
I was seeking to put pressure upon parliament to have its business concluded in time for that particular purpose. I therefore said to his excellency that I hoped that in communicating with His Majesty the King he would ask, as something quite eexceptional but nevertheless something that seemed to me appropriate in the circumstances, whether his majesty would not agree to assent to any bills which might be in readiness for royal assent when he came to Canada, should the business of parliament not then permit of prorogation at the time. What I felt was that members of both houses of parliament would greatly welcome, welcome above all else, the opportunity of meeting with the king himself within the walls of these houses of parliament at the time when his majesty was performing a great act of state in which they also were participating, and it seemed to me that that object could be served either by the presence of his majesty for the purpose of giving the 
royal assent to bills or for the purpose of prorogation of parliament itself. In the United Kingdom the sovereign has not participated in a ceremonial in the nature of royal assent to bills for many years, indeed, not since 1854. As respects the assent to bills, the same procedure has been adopted there as here, namely that of having the royal assent to bills and also prorogation performed with less ceremonial, his majesty's presence being reserved for the opening of parliament. The king notwithstanding has graciously consented, so far as Canada is concerned, appreciating that no single act of state except the opening could mean more to his parliament here than his being present with the members at a ceremonial of the kind, to give, in connection with the royal visit, the royal assent to any bills which may have passed both houses at the time of his majesty's visit, or to prorogue parliament according as circumstances may permit.
I mention this to make perfectly clear in the first place that the last thing the government would wish would be that this parliament should in any way rush its business on account of the royal visit or give other than the fullest attention to public matters, and also to make clear that the government itself has carefully considered this feature.
A final word with regard to the possibility of prorogation. It is true that the time is short. As all hon. members know, more depends upon the disposition and the will of hon. members and upon organization as to what in a given time can be accomplished in this house than upon anything else. We were told at the beginning of the session that we were unduly delaying matters, and the complaint in some quarters was that parliament, because it wished to discuss some matters very fully, did not understand its own business, and that we ought to hurry things along. And ifow that we are making real progress the criticism is that we should not progress at the rate we are, that we ought to see to it that there is an adjournment and after the royal visit come back and take up matters in more leisurely fashion and in detail. I have long since ceased to try to please everyone, but I shall continue to try to bring about that reasonable course of procedure which I believe is likely to commend itself most generally to the members of both houses of parliament.
In conclusion I just wish to say that if we can, by arrangements that are satisfactory to all parties and groups in this house, conclude in time for prorogation by the Friday night preceding the date on which some of us will

Royal Visit and Parliament
have to leave for Quebec, we shall have prorogation when the king is in the capital; otherwise hon. members may look forward to the honour of attending in the senate at that time for the purpose of being present when the royal assent will be given bills by his majesty in person.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition) :
maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext:
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has covered a good deal of ground. I shall merely touch upon two or three points in connection with what he has said.
In the first place may I make it clear that the visit of their majesties to this country is to my mind far above anything in the way of political strategy or politics in any form. In this matter as in that of international relations I feel that there is a duty devolving upon me as leader of the opposition to avoid anything that might have the appearance of political criticism or anything of the sort. The Prime Minister referred to political criticism that he anticipated in regard to. whatever he might do: consequently let me say at once that I have not criticized and shall not in any way criticize any act that refers to the visit of their majesties in Canada. And I am sure that the party which I have the honour to lead will take exactly the same attitude. After all, the government takes the full responsibility of making all the arrangements. The government may be criticized by some sections or individuals in connection with those arrangements, but I do not feel that it is for me to use the visit of their majesties to Canada as an occasion to check or criticize the government or to act in other than a constructive manner, so far as it is possible for me to do so.
In regard to the question of the Prime Minister accompanying their majesties on this journey across Canada, the question is one which seems to me to be partly decided at any rate by the tradition in England. There I understand it is the custom that when his majesty or their majesties visit different parts of the British Isles he is always accompanied by a privy councillor. If the Prime Minister thinks that in Canada that privy councillor should be himself rather than some other minister, that is entirely for the decision of the Prime Minister, and I have no criticism whatever to offer.
May I say also that I am, and our party is, very anxious to facilitate the business of the house. At the same time we are ready to stay here as long as is necessary to do the business of the house. I might say-and this has nothing to do at all with the visit of their majesties-that the government, knowing that
this visit was to take place, might have brought down some of their important legislation a little earlier than they did. However, that is the business of the government and I do not want to appear critical in that regard.
The conduct of affairs here between now and the coming of their majesties, and the question whether or not we adjourn during the time of their visit, are matters that should be governed entirely by consideration for the business of the country. It is not a matter of our convenience or even the convenience of the government. It is the duty of the opposition and of the party to which I belong, which is part of the opposition, to offer intelligent and constructive criticism and to assist in the businesslike and expeditious transaction of the affairs of this country. At the same time, while helping to reach prorogation by the time of the royal visit if we can do so without interfering with the proper carrying out of the business, I believe that neither we nor the government nor any party in this house should hurry so much that any problems that can be dealt with by the government, such as unemployment or provision for youth, would be neglected; neither is it the duty of any of us to pretend that we alone have the care of unemployment or youth at heart. As I said the other day, I think that all hon. members of this house, of all parties, are anxious to see these problems cleared up. After all it must not be forgotten that parliament as parliament can only offer opinions. Parliament cannot do anything; it can suggest, criticize, constructively or even destructively, but it cannot actually do anything; it it the duty of the government to introduce and carry out policies. It is not within the power of any member of this house, other than a member of the government itself, to introduce anything in the way of policy involving the expenditure of money. Therefore we can only offer our suggestions to the best of our ability. So far as this party is able to do so, we shall facilitate the transaction of the business of the house in every way, at the same time not agreeing-as of course we are not asked to agree-in any way to neglect the problems with which the house has to deal.
Regarding the question of adjournment during the visit of their majesties, the Prime Minister was good enough a few days ago to speak to me in my seat in the house and discuss with me in a general way some of the problems which he was facing. At that time I told him that, so far as I was concerned at any rate, and I can speak for the party which I have the honour to lead, we would abstain

Royal Visit and Parliament
from anything in the way of political addresses and would stir up nothing in the way of political strife in any shape or form while their majesties are on the soil of Canada. I believe that is the appropriate and dignified course for us to pursue. When I was speaking to the Prime Minister I told him I thought it was even my duty to avoid taking part in political meetings, and I intend to live up to that duty. There may be local constituency meetings; I do not suppose it would be fair to ask that conventions or matters of local concern should be wholly dispensed with, but so far as national efforts on my part are concerned, as leader of the Conservative party I have no intention of carrying on anything of the kind during the visit of their majesties. I have no intention of making any political speeches across this country or attempting in any way to reach the people on political matters during that period; I believe it is my duty to remain politically silent.
That being so it seems to me it would be very difficult for the house to continue to sit while their majesties are here and while the Prime Minister is travelling across the country with them. After all, it would be practically impossible, during a continued sitting of the house, to avoid matters of dispute or criticism here. So it would appear almost inevitable that during the visit the house must be adjourned, if it is not prorogued, until the king and queen leave the country. That is my stand in the matter.
There was one other point upon which the Prime Minister did not touch, but which has been brought up in the house, and while I am on my .feet I am going to say a word about it. I refer to the question of the proper hospitality to be extended their majesties while they are in this country. Some criticism was offered in my hearing the other day with regard to too great expenditures being made under present conditions in Canada. It is perhaps true that with the present conditions of unemployment and a certain amount of distress in our country there are those who will find fault with the proper entertainment of the king and queen. I am not one of those who take any such attitude. This is the first visit to Canada of the King and Queen of Canada. He is our king; she is our queen. What we spend on any hospitality we may extend to their majesties while they are in this country will be a mere bagatelle compared to the total expenditures of this country. It would mean practically nothing in the relief of unemployment, distress and so on, and I believe our national dignity and our loyalty to their majesties

and to the empire must lead us to extend proper and dignified hospitality to them, in every sense of that word, while they are in this country.
I think I have touched, so far as I have been able to remember them, most of the points dealt with by the Prime Minister, and I hope I have made myself clear in regard to them. However, if something else should come up during the course of this discussion I hope I may be permitted to add a word or two, because I am speaking more or less at random. I am endeavouring to express not only my desire but that of the whole party which I represent, which is that we should facilitate everything that will tend to show our loyalty to their majesties and to the empire, at the same time upholding the dignity and honour of the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext:
I recognize, Mr. Speaker, that our group is not very large, and that what we may think will not have any very great effect in determining the program. However, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has put this matter on the basis of what is convenient and desirable from the point of view of each constituency in Canada.
First of all may I say just a word to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), concerning his reference to a remark I made the other day to the effect that we should not make extravagant expenditures in connection with the royal visit. I still hold that opinion, and hold it very strongly. I do not believe it is necessary, in order to maintain our national dignity, that we go into extravagances; I do not think the amount we spend on this function should be considered in any sense a criterion of the loyalty of the Canadian people. On one occasion, I think on the address in reply, I said that while exhibiting dignity we should not yield to the temptation of extravagance; that we should remember the conditions which prevail in Canada, conditions which are very serious indeed. If by any stretch of the imagination I could put myself in .the place of their majesties I think I should feel well satisfied to have the people of Canada treat me freely and generously as their guest in such way as would befit the Canadian people and the circumstances in which they find themselves.
I quite understand that the Prime Minister is very anxious to prorogue. I think we all are, if that should be at all possible. I think perhaps he has put the matter in such a way as to make it very difficult for us to do anything but prorogue. The right hon. gentleman referred as a precedent to the fact that

Royal Visit and Parliament
Laurier travelled with the Duke of York; but I would point out what I think is the fact, that at that time parliament was not in session, so that the circumstances are somewhat different. Then there is another technical matter. If parliament adjourned from May 12 to June 19, which was one of the suggestions made by the Prime Minister, I presume it would be very difficult for his majesty to assent to any bills on the 17th or 18th.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext: Oh, no. If parliament adjourns on the 12th it will be with the distinct understanding that it will adjourn only until the day fixed for his majesty to give the royal assent; after the royal assent has been given to bills by his majesty, a further adjournment will be taken until the end of the royal visit. I am glad my hon. friend raised that point. I unfortunately had omitted to make the exact position clear. The house will adjourn from Friday night, the 12th, until the following Friday, the 19th, I think it is, when his majesty will be present to give royal assent. Then there will be a further adjournment until after the conclusion of the royal visit. If I am not taking up too much of my hon. friend's time, may I say that I was very careful to endeavour to have the ceremony of royal assent take place, so that members of this parliament, failing its prorogation at the time, would have the honour and privilege of meeting with the king within the walls of these houses of parliament in a great state function. That opportunity will be accorded by means of a royal assent, as it will also be accorded by means of prorogation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext: My difficulty is that if we should adjourn from May 12 to June 19, presumably certain members would go elsewhere.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext: In that regard may I say to my hon. friend that I think every hon. member would wish to be present at the dinner which is being given as a parliamentary dinner in order to enable all hon. members to meet their majesties. That dinner will be held, I think, either the evening of the day on which royal assent is given or the preceding evening. It will be, in fact, on the preceding evening. All hon. members will, I am sure, wish to be in this city during the time their majesties are here.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext:
I am glad that point is made clear. Now with regard to the suggestion made, I think, both by the Prime Minister and by the leader of the opposition, that there should be no acrimonious party
strife during the visit of their majesties, I think I can quite heartily agree. But the suggestion that while the king is here there should be no political discussions is an altogether different matter. I presume that his majesty is quite familiar with political discussions in England, and I think we would be treating him much as he is treated in England if we carried on in much the same way during his visit to this country. I believe he would feel much more at home if that were done than if we were to go into some sort of funeral silence in our public life.
As far as the Prime Minister accompanying the king is concerned, I have no advice to proffer. He suggested, however, that if during the royal tour an emergency should arise, he should be with his majesty. I suggest that if an emergency arose, the place for the Prime Minister is here in parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend will permit me, I did not put it in just that way. I said I thought that his majesty would wish to have with him his Secretary of State for External Affairs who could present to him the sort of information that would be presented to his representative here in the person of the governor general in a similar situation. I do not see how anyone else could fill that particular role.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext: I do not quite see how anyone else except the Prime Minister, who is also Secretary of State for External Affairs, could perform the duties that should be performed in an emergency. I have said also that should an emergency arise, it seems to me that the Prime Minister, as Prime Minister, should not be with his majesty but should be here in the house. I think he would have to return and leave his majesty in the lurch.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext: The house will not be sitting.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext:
With regard to our own position, our little group has no intention or desire to obstruct the business of the house in the slightest between now and the time their majesties arrive. We have been accused by some of wanting to carry on a filibuster or something of the kind, but no such intention has been in our minds. I have said to the Prime Minister that we believe that the business before this parliament should be concluded. We are particularly interested in the unemployment question, in the western grain matter, in the world situation and in national defence policies, and even the coming of their majesties should not interfere with the proper conduct of the business of this
Royal Visit and Parliament

house. I believe that our greatest contribution to the British empire, if you will, will be to carry on the business of this house for which we were elected. I have yet to be convinced by the Prime Minister or by the eloquent words of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) that we should alter that stand.
The Prime Minister suggests as a second alternative that we should have an adjournment of between five and six weeks. I cannot see that that is necessary. I have not had a chance to consult my own colleagues with regard to this proposal, but it would seem to me that an adjournment of about ten days might suffice if we do not succeed in reaching prorogation. I do not see why we should adjourn for the full period of their majesties' visit. If necessary, this or that member could slip away for a day or so and then return to the house. I venture to suggest that in the meantime we should likely have in the house about as large a representation of members as we frequently have at ordinary times.
I cannot see that any argument so far advanced is sufficient to warrant us, first, in proroguing before full consideration has been given to all business, or, second, having a prolonged adjournment in case prorogation is not possible. It would seem to me to be much more in keeping if we carried on our business as usual, adjourned for say ten days, and then came back and finished our business with due decorum. I do not think their majesties would be slighted by our so doing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members of this group I think I can safely say that we are willing, I might even say anxious, to do everything in our power to expedite the business of the house so as to be through by the time the king arrives. There are, of course, certain measures before us of a most contentious nature, those with regard to grain especially, which we will feel it our bounden duty to oppose unless they are changed from the form in which they appear on the order paper at the present time. If the business of the house cannot be completed by the time the king arrives, we do not think it is necessary to have such a long adjournment as that suggested by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). As far as the Prime Minister personally is concerned, I feel that it would be proper that he should accompany the king during the royal tour of Canada. An adjournment of five or six days, or perhaps ten, would be long enough. It should not be necessary for more than a certain number of members to be absent at any one time. The

Trans-Canada Air Lines is now in operation and it is possible for hon. members to travel from one end of the dominion to the other in a very short time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may be permitted to say a word, since on one or two occasions I have been reported in the press as being critical of the arrangements that have been made. May I say at the outset that I think every one of us desires that everything should be done in connection with the royal visit to convey to their majesties the impression that their visit is welcomed and that the Canadian people are prepared to do all that is possible to show their respect to the royal couple. But there is a tremendous amount of business yet to be done. This is the fourth session of the present parliament and there are rumours of a general election. Two years ago we prorogued in order that representatives of Canada might attend, and properly so, their majesties' coronation.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was speaking I jotted down just a few of the matters which in my opinion, and in the opinion of my constituents, are worthy of the most careful consideration. The budget is to be introduced tomorrow. I do not know what it will contain, but if some things are not in the budget, I know my constituents will be disappointed. Then we have the problems of national defence and external affairs, which I believe are pressing upon the minds of practically all Canadian people at this time. My constituents being in a wheat producing area, are vitally interested in the wheat bills now before the house, and I am sure they desire that every opportunity shall be given to hon. members of this house to discuss them fully. They desire also that every consideration should be given by the government to the representations made by delegations which are coming to this parliament in connection with these matters. The same thing applies to other measures which have been introduced by the minister dealing with other phases of agricultural marketing.
Then there is the problem we have just been discussing, the grave problem of unemployment and the rehabilitation of youth. I do not intend to labour the matter at this time, because it received a thorough airing last week. We have been expecting and hoping that before this parliament should be dissolved, certain constitutional matters might be decided in order that we might be able to look forward to certain remedial legislation which is so long overdue. I have felt and still feel that we should conduct the business

Royal Visit and Parliament
of the house in the ordinary way, and that probably a short adjournment would meet the situation. As far as the Prime Minister accompanying their majesties is concerned, I think that should be done as far as possible. But after all, the governor general, who is the representative of his majesty in the dominion of Canada, does from time to time travel across the country, and it is not felt essential that he should be accompanied by the Prime Minister in order that he might be given advice regarding matters which may arise and in connection with which the Prime Minister normally advises the governor general. I have felt that members of the privy council might substitute for the Prime Minister in the house and on the tour, and that we might proceed with the business of parliament. Since I have made that criticism outside of the house and the Prime Minister has invited anyone to give his expression of opinion, I thought it my duty to express here what I have said outside. In addition to the legislation before the house there are important committees sitting, one dealing with amendments to the grain act, another with the civil service superannuation, and others with other important matters, and I feel strongly that it would be impossible so to expedite business that we might prorogue on their majesties' arrival. I am in favour personally of treating their majesties with every respect, but at the same time of conducting the business of his majesty properly in this parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has asked for the individual opinions of members of parliament who feel themselves in a position to express the views of their constituents. I have been in Montreal more or less recently and have heard a great deal of discussion of the matters we are discussing here this afternoon, and the general opinion expressed was that it was for the Prime Minister himself to decide as to his duty and responsibility in accompanying his majesty throughout Canada on the royal visit. It was also remarked, as a mere incident, that certainly the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom did not always regard it as his duty to accompany his majesty when visiting Northern Ireland or Scotland.
Moreover, the suggestion was made that if the Prime Minister felt it to be his duty to accompany their majesties, that was no reason why parliament should adjourn in the meantime, but rather that the business of parliament should go on. It might proceed, with all due respect to the Prime Minister, in his absence. I remember other occasions when the Prime Minister was not present for weeks, and when
the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) as Acting Prime Minister, led the house with singular aptitude, suavity and success. There is a strong feeling in the city from which I come that in the present case one or more of the Prime Minister's colleagues might efficiently and effectively lead the house if the Prime Minister felt it his duty to be absent for six weeks. That would enable members to attend to the business of the country in the absence of the Prime Minister.
So far as I am concerned I do not think it possible for us, doing our best, to conclude the business of parliament in fourteen days of discussion, and fourteen days is about all that would be left for discussion if the course which the Prime Minister suggests were followed. It is useless to crowd the business of the house, and I think parliament should sit until it has completed its business. The strain of the work in the last three years of parliament has been as great as in any other year I have been in the house, and I remember years when repeatedly I left the house as daylight broke after an all-night session. But the mortality among members of this house, since the first session of this parliament, is so great as to indicate that we are here having many duties to perform and concerned with many anxieties.
I do not think the Prime Minister really suggested that it would be necessary for him as Secretary of State for External Affairs to be present with his majesty. Certainly I have no doubt that his majesty will be well advised by his ministers at Westminster from day to day, through his private secretaries and his staff, as to the progress of critical international affairs. It would be very interesting for him to have the opinion of the Prime Minister with respect to them, an opinion which is denied to us so frequently, but that could be arranged otherwise.
Let the Prime Minister attend or not attend during the whole of their majesties' tour, as he conscientiously believes it his duty to do, and no one can do otherwise than respect his judgment in that regard. But certainly the discussions which we have in this house, no matter how acrimonious they may be, would not alarm his majesty; for he doubtless keeps himself en rapport with the proceedings of parliament at Westminster. Here we would say nothing to shock his majesty, but we would, I trust, enter upon an intelligent discussion of the issues which are presented. Parliament is sitting for that purpose. I have no sympathy with the idea that appears in the press so frequently that parliament should prorogue after a session of three or four weeks. Those who make that
Royal Visit and Parliament

criticism have little knowledge of the daily work that is done by members of parliament, in the committees and in this house, during the session. It is for us to decide as to the conduct of business here. It is for the Prime Minister to decide as to the leadership of the house in his absence. Personally I trust that he will arrange for that leadership during such time as he may be absent during the royal visit.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext:
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has asked for views. He has heard from the leaders and statesmen of various parties. Perhaps he would be interested in hearing from one of the common rank and file. I speak only for myself. I have had no intimation or request or advice from home as regards my attitude in this matter, and therefore I have to use my own poor judgment. But it would be this, and I think I know the sentiments of the people I represent. They would be entirely agreeable; more than agreeable I think, to see the Prime Minister attend his majesty during his visit. I think we should be lacking in courtesy to the king if that were not done as well as lacking in our own self-respect.
But the Prime Minister did not explore to the extent I should have liked him to do the alternative suggested by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). I would hope it might be possible to adjourn for a week during the king's stay in Ottawa, and then continue with the business of the house. That would seem to me to meet the situation on all sides, and it would avoid any suggestion that we were rushing prorogation. On the other hand it would mean that we would not be sitting here in the heat of summer. Imagine what the health and tempers would be like of 245 men sitting here in the middle of July and later. I certainly think that if it could be done, the suggestion made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George should be carried out-that the Prime Minister attend, as I would almost say it is his duty to attend, His Majesty the King while in Canada, but that following his majesty's visit to Ottawa the house go on with its business.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext:
Occupying this seat as I do for want of a better, I do not wish it to be assumed by inference that I necessarily follow the views of those in front of me. To me, royalty is a very important part of our thinking as a people. Our king, to me, is a symbol of the soul of the people, and I believe that we best express our democracy when we regard him as such. He comes

to us on an auspicious occasion, and I feel that every sign of respect should be shown him, because he so clearly represents the highest and the best that are in ourselves.
I have agreed with practically all that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said. The more we do to show our duty and our respect, our loyalty and our sincerity to the symbol of the soul of ourselves, the better we shall be for it. As to the length of the adjournment, I have no particular view, but I hope that the man who gives out the weather reports will try to give us cool nights as long as we stay here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-ROYAL VISIT AND PROCEEDINGS OF PARLIAMENT IN RELATION THERETO
speechtext:
I do not think it is necessary for me to add more than a word to what I have already said, except as an expression of thanks to hon. members of all parties for their courtesy in extending their views in the manner in which they have. As the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has said, in the last analysis the decision has to be made by the Prime Minister himself as to what he himself is to do, and, to some extent, as to what is to be done with respect to parliament in the matter of its proceedings. In this connection, however, let me assure the house that I have followed, as I have sought to do ever since I have held my present office, the counsel and advice of those who sit around me in the cabinet. The decision reached commends itself to the members of the government generally. We have been at one in regard to the attitude that should be taken by myself with respect to accompanying the king, and it is out of that collective wisdom as well as from a sense of personal responsibility which, in the circumstances, I cannot escape, that I have felt it was the right decision to make.
The whole position is without precedent. That is what has made it so difficult; and, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) has just said, there is bound to be a great deal of criticism of many of the things which may be done or left undone in the course of the royal visit. I hope hon. members and the people generally will be generous enough to realize that the fact that there has been no precedent of the kind in the history of this country has made it additionally difficult to satisfy all views with respect to what should be done in regard to many matters which are very important and material. I can assure hon. members, however, that no end of thought and care has been given to all these matters, and that every effort has been made to reach decisions in the light of what seemed to be the view which would most commend itself to the people of Canada.

Royal Visit and Parliament
In the matter of being attended by one of his ministers, probably all will agree that his majesty's own views and wishes should be taken into account. In that connection I may refer the house to the communication which appeared in the press a day or two ago, in which it was stated that his majesty had invited me to accompany him as minister in attendance during his visit to the United States. I may say that the invitation came to me in a communication written by his majesty himself. I believe it is the custom for the king, when going abroad, to decide first of all whether or not he will be accompanied by a minister, and his majesty reaches his own decision as to what may be most advisable in the circumstances. It need scarcely be said that I felt very greatly honoured when I received his majesty's letter, but I accept the honour as one which is intended by his majesty as a recognition of the position which Canada has attained as one of the nations of the British commonwealth equal in status in all aspects of her domestic and external affairs with the United Kingdom itself. I am sure that this has been the circumstance which has weighed most in the mind of his majesty in inviting the Prime Minister of Canada as Prime Minister to accompany him when he visits the United States. His majesty's views should, I submit, be considered with respect to his visit in Canada as well as to the country to the south. In all respects I shall seek to see that as far as possible they are wholly met.
Just this further word about the matter of an adjournment for a short time as against adjournment for a longer time. I believe I have made it clear that the consideration which to me is of most concern is the wish of hon. members themselves. I believe that members of parliament generally will wish to be in the parts of the country from which they come when their majesties are visiting those particular parts. But further, I believe the public will wish to have the opportunity to view the proceedings of parliament dispassionately and calmly, and I question very much if they will have that opportunity through the press reports as they will necessarily appear at the time of their majesties' visit. I do not mean by that that there will not be adequate reports, but I believe that I have some appreciation of where the centre of public interest will be during the period of their majesties' visit. I am pretty sure that a great deal of attention will be given to
all aspects of the royal visit, and that the proceedings of parliament will be much better reported and more closely followed at a time when their majesties are not in the country. It hardly covers the ground to say that in England parliament proceeds in a normal way, or that, for example, in Canada the governor general himself is not accompanied on all occasions by a minister of the crown. The parallel is not a true one. This is the first time that the king and queen have ever visited this country. It is an historic occasion; it is one without precedent in the history of the British empire; it is an event of world-wide interest and concern. These special circumstances have to be specially considered.
iMay I just add, what I think must be obvious, that having had the obligations and the duties which rest upon the leader of a political party for the length of time that I have had them, and the anxieties which, at least during the past few months, have accompanied them, I personally am not at all anxious to add to the strain of those anxieties and responsibilities the additional ones which necessarily will come in travelling through the country with members of the royal party rather than remaining here and sharing time and responsibility with hon. members in this house. I mention this only because I feel it is due to hon. members to know, having in mind the fact that I am to accompany their majesties throughout their tour, that if that duty is to be performed, I may have to ask the house to allow me, even Jjefore the time of adjournment or prorogation, at least a day or two in which to secure a much needed rest, and to reach some decisions and to make some arrangements which there has not thus far been an opportunity to make in connection with the royal tour.
Motion withdrawn.
