subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE IN OFFICE FOR THREE YEARS FROM JANUARY 7, 1940

speechtext:
Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 91, respecting the Chief Justice of Canada.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 1-Term of office.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE IN OFFICE FOR THREE YEARS FROM JANUARY 7, 1940
speechtext:
As I suppose some explanation of this bill is in order, I may say that the present Chief Justice of Canada, as members of the committee know, is a great jurist, one of the finest legal minds in the British commonwealth, and the equal of any legal mind in the world. He has made a reputation not only in Canada but even when he sits as a member of his majesty's privy council. Apart from that, he is an eminent gentleman enjoying the confidence of Canadians throughout the land.
Under the law as it is, the chief justice would have to retire in January next, because he will then have reached the age of seventy-five. It was a relief to me, I must say, when I asked him on behalf of the government to give his services for a longer period, that he undertook to do so, and I am grateful to him. I am therefore expressing not only my thanks but those of the country to the chief justice, who has felt it his duty to accept an extension of his term. As a rule, the law that compels retirement at seventy-five is a good one, but he is an exceptional man, and we are in exceptional circumstances so far as the Supreme Court of Canada is concerned.
The chief justice has accepted from a high sense of duty. He could retire with his full salary, his full pension, and he serves without any benefit, financial or otherwise. He is simply undertaking to serve the Dominion of Canada.
This bill is also a measure of economy, because if the chief justice were retiring we should have to pay him his full salary as well as the salary of his successor. Under the circumstances I am sure I am expressing the views of members of the committee in asking that the bill be made law.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE IN OFFICE FOR THREE YEARS FROM JANUARY 7, 1940
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words in regard to the proposal to extend for three years the term of the Chief Justice, Sir Lyman Duff. In this connection I wish to compliment the government. I rarely pay them compliments but this is one of the few occasions on which I can do so. I favour 
this bill enthusiastically. I agree entirely with what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has said, in so far as one who is not a lawyer can participate in a discussion of the qualifications of the chief justice.
I have had many contacts with Sir Lyman Duff and have heard his qualifications very widely discussed as a judge and as a lawyer, and I wish to endorse fully the idea of extending his term. After hearing Sir Lyman Duff discussed for many years, and having heard lawyers of eminence describe his qualifications, I have come to the conclusion that he is a great chief justice, a great lawyer and a great scholar. He has intellectual attainments of the highest order. Since the time he was appointed to the privy council in 1918, his judgments, I am informed, have been recognized and cited with approval not only in the United Kingdom but throughout the whole British commonwealth of nations.
I have heard Sir Lyman Duff described by one lawyer as having a broad and original grasp of legal principles, and he is considered by .the same lawyer as the greatest judge ever to have held a seat on the bench in any of the British dominions. That is very high praise indeed, and from all my knowledge it is apparently well deserved. The other day the Ottawa Journal, in an admirable editorial discussing the subject of this bill, Sir Lyman Duff, described him as balanced, penetrating, scholarly, one of the empire's great jurists, and compared him to the late Oliver Wendell Holmes, a former justice of the Supreme Court of the United States. I was greatly interested in that, because I remember when Oliver Wendell Holmes died, high praise was heaped on his qualifications as a justice of the Supreme Court of the United States. There were many comments on the wonderful work he had done, with particular reference to his ability to outline in magnificent language his judgments in the various cases that had come before him. That brought back to my mind some of my early reading as a young doctor many years ago. Some of the most delightful passages in literature I found in the writings of the elder Oliver Wendell Holmes, the father of the late Mr. Justice Holmes, a doctor-a man of my own profession. He wrote The Autocrat of the Breakfast-table and the Professor at the Breakfast-table. I greatly enjoyed these charming and delightful examples of literature, and I presume Mr. Justice Holmes inherited that gift of writing from his father.
From all that I can gather, Sir Lyman is one of the truly great Canadians. I had a direct contact with him, apart from social

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
intercourse, when I appointed him as chairman of what was known as the Duff commission on railways. During the time he presided over that commission both he and the commission did splendid work, but he was the guiding force behind the decisions of the commission and it was his skill that very largely helped to make those decisions clear-cut and well-balanced. I think that commission did splendid work, work which has been all too quickly forgotten. When people are discussing the railway situation they would do well to go back to the report of the Duff commission and study the conclusions at which that commission arrived.
In supporting the Minister of Justice in the proposal embodied in this bill L feel that I am doing what I think should be done always, namely, to keep the bench above anything in the way of politics. The appointments made should always be of the highest order; in that connection there is reposed in the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice a most important trust, because the freedom and liberty of the subject are confided to the care of our courts. Canada's reputation, on this continent at any rate, as a law-abiding country, one in which the ordinary citizen has a deep respect for the law, is largely due to the high standing of its judiciary in its various branches.
I heartily endorse the action of the Minister of Justice in the extension of the term of office of Sir Lyman Duff. I sincerely hope that when the next three years have passed and it is again time for Sir Lyman's term to be extended, I as prime minister may suggest to my minister of justice an extension for another three years.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

speechtext: Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS moved the third reading of Bill No. 96, to assist in the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
The other day I rose to make a few remarks in committee and was called to order because of the insistence of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) on strict adherence to the rules of procedure. I felt at the time that I was entirely within my rights, but naturally I
had to defer to the ruling of the chairman. At this time I do not intend to do what the minister did a few days ago. If I wanted to stand on my rights I could go on speaking for several hours, but such is not my intention. I think that if the rules of the house were applied more liberally we would perhaps make just as much headway as we do by seeking to apply them too rigidly.
I do not wish to speak at greater length than it is usual for me to speak in this chamber-forty minutes. The most that can be said for long speeches is the time they take up; long speeches usually are noted rather for length than for breadth. Consequently I shall keep to the usual time in the observations I intend to make and limit myself in that respect if I possibly can.
I said the other day that the one thing that impressed me during the discussion on the unemployment situation in this chamber last week was that the government really have nothing in the way of effective remedies to deal with the problem. For the past three and a half years the Minister of Labour has worked hard, and I think he is to-day a rather disappointed man by mason of the lack of success of his policies so far. It cannot be said that they have been effective in dealing with unemployment in Canada. I think it can be shown, and the minister will be the first to admit, that there are about as many people out of work at the present time as there were when the present government assumed office in 1935. So that if we have to take the number of unemployed as a criterion of the success or failure of the government, the least one can say is that the policies of the government up to now have not been successful.
The other thing that struck me forcibly was the hostility that some hon. members of the Liberal party showed towards the unemployed. I was sorry indeed to see some hon. members applaud the statements made in that regard. I do not intend to repeat them, but I feel that as a mere matter of judgment hon. members who in a moment of enthusiasm applauded the remarks of the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Blair) probably felt sorry on further reflection.
This problem of unemployment has been with us from the beginning of 1930. During that year it became more and more acute. About this time nine years ago I moved a resolution in this house asking the government to take immediate steps to deal with the problem, because anyone at that time who had any understanding of the economics of the situation could not fail to realize that we were
3106	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
on the eve of a tremendously difficult situation, faced as we were by the collapse which subsequently occurred. The government of that day thought there was very little in the way of unemployment, and what there was could be taken care of by the local authorities; so that they did nothing. Then an election came round, and we had a complete change of government, no doubt due to a very large extent to the economic conditions which then prevailed.
In 1930 the new government assumed office. It is well to bear in mind some of the things that the government did even in 1930 to deal with this problem, because they assume a certain importance in view of what the government is attempting to do at the present time. Some hon. members to my immediate right will say: Well, let us forget what happened between 1930 and 1935. But I am not one who thinks we should forget those things. Not that I am unwilling to forgive them, but to forget is another thing, because from the experience of the past we should gain at least some understanding of the problems facing us now.
During the years 1930 to 1935, when the Liberal party were in opposition, they had opportunity of understanding the problem, and when they came into power in 1935 they should have been in a better position to deal with it than was the government of 1930. When that government took office in the fall of 1930 a special session of parliament was called to deal with unemployment and I think it is well that I should read a brief extract from the speech from the throne of September 8, 1930. The following was submitted through His Excellency the Governor General:
The necessity for dealing with exceptional economic conditions with the resultant unemployment has induced me to summon you at an earlier date than would otherwise be necessary.
Measures will be submitted for your consideration, including amendments to the Customs Act and the Customs Tariff, which it is anticipated will do much to meet the unusual conditions which now prevail.
What I want to point out is that in the fall of 1930 the government of the day thought that by a manipulation of the tariff and by amendments to the Customs Act, which meant heavy dumping duties, they could cure the unemployment situation. Subsequent events showed the fallacy of that contention. Even yet, however, I hear some of my hon. friends of the Conservative party insist that by increasing tariffs you can cure unemployment. If I thought the remedy was as simple as all that, I should hold up my hands every time for increasing the tariff.

In the speech from the throne the following year, submitted to parliament through His Excellency the Governor General on Thursday, March 12, 1931, I find the following language:
It will be your privilege to consider certain measures designed by my ministers to ameliorate existing conditions, to provide further means by which our people may go forward to achieve a prosperity heretofore unattained and to furnish them with all possible safeguards against a recurrence of the present subordination to world forces.
Then follow these words:
The problems which stand between us and ultimate prosperity are manifold and great. To be effectually met, they must first be understood. Confusion between cause and effect will but delay their solution. My government has explored the origins of our difficulties and is firmly of the belief that many of our problems do not arise out of world wide depression, but are antecedent to it; and that domestic factors have also largely determined the degree of economic distress from which this country is suffering.
It was this belief which impelled my ministers at the emergency session of parliament held in September last to remove one of the root weaknesses in our industrial system by effecting such then possible changes in the tariff as would, in their opinion, provide substantial security against harmful world conditions.
In other words, it was felt by the government then in power, at the beginning of 1931, that the adjustments in the tariff by themselves would be sufficient to meet economic conditions and bring a measure of prosperity to the people of Canada.
On February 4, 1932, however, we had another speech from the throne, after we had experimented with the tariff for eighteen months. In that speech we find these words:
World conditions are beyond the control of the Canadian people.
Evidently it was felt by the government of the day, after eighteen months in office, that tariff adjustments were not a solution of the economic difficulties from which we were suffering at the time. - In 1932 and 1933 we had about the worst depression this country has ever known. During that period I think the unemployed numbered in the neighbourhood of two-thirds of a million people. In 1934 and 1935, however, the number was very considerably decreased, until I believe in 1935 those out of work could be said to be about equal in number to those out of work at the present time. In other words a measure of increased production which took place in 1933, 1934 and 1935 absorbed fairly large numbers of those who were then out of work. I do not intend to go into the reasons for that now; I may deal with them later on.
In 1935 there was a change of government, but prior to that change we had what we

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
called the new deal legislation of the then government, legislation of which our group approved in the main and for which we voted. The question arises, why did the Conservative party bring in all that kind of legislation in 1934 and 1935? In my opinion it was brought in because it had been proven conclusively in the years that had passed that the tariff remedies which were being applied were no remedies at all under the circumstances, and perforce the government had to turn, to new methods of dealing with the situation.
Then we had the advent of the. Liberal party in 1935. When they came to power there was still a serious condition of unemployment. Certain pledges were made to the people by the Liberal party, and I do not think it would be out of place, in view of the fact that this may be the last session of parliament before another election, if at this time I should remind the Liberal party of some of the pledges it then made to the people.
Speaking in Vancouver on August 5, the present Prime Minister said he would appoint a national commission to deal with the problem of unemployment, and he chided the then prime minister with starting too late to deal with the problem of unemployment. This is what he said:
The national commission would require the cooperation of provincial governments and municipalities, and this it could readily obtain as all provincial governments but one are Liberal.
Is not the election of a Liberal government at Ottawa the sanest sort of approach to a national government? Mr. King asked. With provincial and federal governments all Liberal, friction would end. There would be thoroughgoing cooperation and constitutional difficulties would disappear with an ease which might astonish J. S. Woodsworth, the C.C.F. leader.
I wonder if those constitutional difficulties have disappeared. I wonder if to-day we have the cooperation between the federal and provincial governments that was foreshadowed by the Prime Minister at that time. Then the right hon. gentleman went on to say:
"In order to conceal the growing magnitude of the problem and at the same time its own growing incapacity to deal with it, the government either did not seek to obtain information which at all times should have been available to the people's representatives in parliament, or had deliberately withheld such information as it had from them." In 1930, the Liberal leader continued, Premier Bennett estimated there were 117,000 unemployed in Canada. The census of 1931 placed the number at 393,000. The most conservative estimate to-day-
That was in 1935.
-places it at 400,000. "It is at least well within the mark to say that the number of unemployed in Canada to-day is four times what it was when the Bennett government assumed office."
If at that time the present Prime Minister held it strongly against the then government that they were unfit to be returned for a further period because there were 400,000 people out of work, what shall I say as far as this government is concerned when we have more than that number unemployed at the present time?
Let me refer to some of the promises that were made. It is rather difficult for those of us who are in opposition to compete with the promises of a party that is looking to the attainment of power. During the last election I remember seeing everywhere I went in the city of Winnipeg cards bearing this inscription:
Vote for the Liberal party and work and wages.
What have the people of Canada to-day? They have neither work nor wages. Leaflets were distributed, probably by the hundreds of thousands, containing the following statement:
Tory policies cannot end unemployment. Vote Liberal.
The inference there was that the Tory policies could not end unemployment, but that if the people voted for the Liberals, the Liberal policies certainly would end unem-ploment. These leaflets were no doubt going out by the million, throughout the country. I quote another statement of the policy of the Liberal party:
The Liberal party believes unemployment is Canada's most urgent national problem. It would deal with the present emergency conditions through a representative national commission, which would cooperate with the provinces and municipalities in the administration of unemployment relief and in an endeavour to provide work for the unemployed.
As permanent measures the Liberal party is pledged to introduce policies which will serve to provide employment by reviving industry and trade; and to introduce a national system of unemployment insurance.
As yet we have had neither of these. Then they say further in this leaflet which was issued by the National Liberal Federation:
To prevent exploitation of the public through the sale of watered stocks and worthless securities, it believes an investment control board should be established, with supervision of issues of securities by companies incorporated under federal charters.
We have not that. Then I come to a promise which is much wider in its implication than any of those I have just mentioned. I quote:
The Liberal party believes that industrial reconstruction is the problem of the future. It will seek in industrial relations, as opportunity offers, to give to workers and consumers a larger share in the government of industry.
What has the government done, what has the government even attempted to do, to
3108	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
implement that promise made by the Prime Minister on the floor of this house on February 27, 1933? Nothing whatsoever. The minister has told us he is quite prepared to go to the country on the record of his government on this problem of unemployment. He does not have to tell this house a story of that kind. The government must go to the country on the record, because they have no other possible alternative. Then we find this further statement:
The Liberal party recognizes that the problem of distribution has become more important than that of production, and believe that personality is more sacred than property. It will devote itself to finding ways and means of effecting a fair and just distribution of wealth with increasing regard to human need, to the furtherance of social justice, and to the promotion of the common good.
What legislation has this government introduced during the last four sessions of parliament to implement any of the pledges made by the Liberal party during the last election or upon the floor of this house? I do not think we can find anything in any legislation that will bring about a more equitable distribution of our wealth than we had at the time the Liberal party came into power. It will be conceded by practically every hon. member of this house that unemployment and the economic conditions which prevail in this country present the most pressing problems that this parliament and the government have to face. Yet nothing of a concrete nature has been done to grapple with these questions. In connection with constitutional questions, a commission was appointed to investigate and report. No doubt it will bring in a report in which very few people, comparatively speaking, will be interested. If the government had shown the same energy in appointing some body to deal effectively with economic conditions, it is quite possible that such a body would have performed a much more useful function than will the commission appointed to deal with the constitutional questions of the day.
I represent a fairly large industrial constituency, and I can take hon. members to large areas in my constituency where people are practically living on relief. I do not want to see people living on relief week in and week out, month in and month out, and year in and year out. I want to see our people useful and producing citizens. They have not the opportunities to-day, and so far the present government has taken no effective action to give our people even some hope for the immediate future. Looking back over the record of the government for the past four years I cannot say that the members 
of the government have not worked hard. I do not think there is a harder working minister in the cabinet than the Minister of Labour. He has worked hard and conscientiously, but I think he will be the first to admit that up to now the policies which have been pursued have not been productive of good results; at least they have not coped effectively with the problem of unemployment.
Unemployment has been recognized by the government as being the most important problem facing the country. It has been so recognized in the speeches from the throne which have been delivered since 1936. In the speech from the throne of that year, the first after this government was elected, appears this statement:
Unemployment continues to be Canada's most urgent national problem. While there is an increase in the number of persons employed, the number of those on relief shows no abatement.
I am not going to blame the government for the conditions that prevailed at the beginning of 1936. I did not expect that there would be any change in the early part of that year, because the government had not had an opportunity to put into effect the policies which they thought were going to be effective. In 1937 the government, through His Excellency the Governor General, made this statement in the speech from the throne:
The year just closed has witnessed a Bteady improvement in conditions throughout Canada, and has borne testimony to the beneficial effects of the fiscal policies of the administration, and of other methods employed to achieve national recovery. A very definite restoration of confidence is in itself an augury of the continuance of recovery.
I wonder if the Minister of Labour will contend to-day that the fiscal policies of the government were responsible for the economic recovery which took place in 1936. Personally I cannot give any credit to the fiscal policies of this government for bringing about those changes. I will just mention in passing that the United States was spending billions and billions of dollars in an effort to improve the economic conditions of that country and we in Canada benefited to a fairly large extent from what was being done in the United States, because that country in many ways is a good customer of ours.
The speech from the throne delivered in 1938, which dealt with conditions in 1937, contained the following:
It is gratifying to note that, during the past year, there has been a further substantial advance in Canada's economic recovery. Revenues have reached new levels. Trade with other countries has materially expanded. There has been a general increase in employment and a marked decrease in the numbers receiving unemployment aid.

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
According to the speech from the throne the fiscal policies, so-called, of the government were still having their effect and we were doing fairly well here in Canada.
In the speech from the throne delivered this year we find this statement:
Unemployment in Canada continues to receive the unremitting attention of local, provincial and federal authorities.
Then they deal with the British North America Act, and further on they say:
In Canada, the problem of unemployment has been aggravated in recent years by recurrent crop failures-
With that statement I am in complete accord.
-in the western provinces, and by the serious business recession experienced in the last year in other parts of the world.
In other words, the fiscal policies of the government had ceased to be effective, just as was the case under the Conservative government in the years 1931, 1932 and 1933, when their fiscal policies showed no sign of ameliorating conditions. The fiscal policies of this government in the years of expanding markets are all right; but in years of contracting markets, it is not their fiscal policies that are to blame, they now tell us, but world conditions.
Then they go on to deal with the problem of dominion-provincial relations, and say:
In accordance with the purpose for which the commission was instituted, its report will provide the basis for, and the material essential to the deliberations of a national conference, at which, among the important subjects to be dealt with, will be the problem of unemployment and social services generally. The government have not altered their view that a national unemployment insurance scheme is essential to a permanent policy of meeting the problem of unemployment.
With that I am wholly in disagreement. I do not think that unemployment insurance will meet the problems of unemployment. It will meet some of the problems arising out of unemployment by granting insurance benefits to those who happen to be insured and out of work, but in no sense will it solve the problem of unemployment.
Then we are to have another conference. I thought this government had got away from the idea of conferences but it appears they are still determined to have another conference when the Rowell commission reports, and what will come out of it I suppose will be what has come out of other conferences-talk, talk, talk, and no action.
Then further:
To this end it is proposed further to expand the government's long range program of public undertakings. In pursuance of the policy of
the active encouragement of employment, it is also proposed to undertake, with provincial cooperation, to provide assistance to municipalities which, as an alternative to the provision of direct relief, desire to expand their normal programs of civic improvements.
Further:
In order to avert economic disaster to a large part of our population, my ministers, under the terms of the Wheat Board Act, approved, for the current crop year, an initial payment for wheat as recommended by the board.
What is the condition of the country at the present time? While I do not blame the government entirely for present conditions, there is no one else who can assume the responsibility, and conditions to-day, I submit, are in some respects infinitely worse than they were in 1935. Only this past year we have been called upon to grant a bonus to the producers of grain in the west amounting to approximately fifty million dollars. That was not required in 1935. A similar bonus is being demanded by the western wheat growers for this year. We have deficits on our national railway, resulting from economic conditions, amounting to approximately fifty million dollars a year. We are asked to provide subsidies here and there, such as, for the fishing industry and for many other industries. People are asking for grants in aid of one thing and another. I wonder how any country can continue to grant subsidies and live on deficits. In other words we are trying to pull ourselves up by our bootstraps, and it simply cannot be done.
I come to the question of international trade. I know that the Minister of Labour for a number of years has held international trade as one of his pet theories for improving the economic conditions which prevail in Canada. Every hon. member of this house wants to see international trade expand. We all want more trade; for the more trade there is in the world the better it should be for all concerned. But suppose other nations say to us in Canada: We do not want your surplus goods. What are we to do? Are we to sit in our seats here and do nothing because people of other nations say they do not want our surplus commodities? If our granaries are full to overflowing with wheat and our packing plants are filled with foodstuffs that other nations do not want to buy from us, is that any reason why our people should go without the necessities of life? Suppose the minister had his cupboards in his own home filled with all the foodstuffs and clothing he required, and had no money in his pocket to buy goods, would he wait until somebody came along and gave him a dole, or would he go to his own cupboards for the essentials of life that he required? The logical thing for

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
him to do would be to go to his own cupboards, of course, and take the things that he wanted for himself and his family. That is what I have advocated in this house for a great number of years. With our granaries full to overflowing and our packing plants and warehouses and factories filled with goods for which we can find no market abroad, there is no reason why the people at home should go without the essentials of life. In other words, as was well said by the Prime Minister in this house, and as I said a few moments ago, it is no longer a question of production, of putting more people to work to produce more wealth that we are not allowed to consume; it is a question of a fairer distribution of the wealth that is being produced.
But, so far the government has taken no steps to bring that about, and until such time as we in Canada try to bring about a fairer distribution of our wealth production, we shall never solve the problems which confront us. It is of no use to attribute our domestic problems to lack of international trade. Do not let us blame somebody else for our own shortcomings. If we are short of international trade, let us try to develop an internal economy which will satisfy to the best of our ability our own population, and I believe that we here in Canada can secure for our own people a fairly high standard of living if we will only give them the opportunity to work and consume the goods which they can produce.
The minister and those associated with him have told us on more than one occasion about the changes that have taken place in Europe. It is true that during recent years and even within the past few months great changes have been made in the physical map of Europe, but in addition to those physical changes there have also been great changes in the economic map of Europe. The old economic way of doing things has gone in the greater part of Europe. All the totalitarian states in Europe have thrown into the discard capitalism as we knew it in the early part of this century. They are exploring new economic paths. They are trying to become selfsufficient. They do not want our goods. We must recognize these facts. Far be it from me to say that I approve what the totalitarian states in Europe are doing. But we have to recognize the facts, and the one way to recognize them is by attempting here in Canada to solve our problems as best we can, remembering the vast amount of wealth which the dominion contains.

The old theory that low prices increase consumption of goods has pretty well gone into the discard. In western Canada our farmers are trying to sell their grain at prices representing not much more than one half the cost of production, yet they are unable to find a market. If a low price created a greater demand, our grain would have been consumed long since and we should have had no problem so far as a surplus is concerned.
Here is another point which the minister, who is an economist of repute, should bear in mind. We are living in an age when capitalism has practically ceased to expand; indeed the tendency is in the other direction as the markets of the world become fewer and more limited. We must recognize that condition when we are considering policies intended to solve unemployment by finding markets in other parts of the world. The former government attempted that same thing, although in doing so .they used stronger language than the present government has used: for example, Mr. Bennett, when prime minister, said they would blast their way into the markets of the world. But that policy of blasting was no more successful than the present government's policy has been.
In view of the wealth Canada has at her disposal, the large number of people who, though willing, are unable to work, the immense resources which are at our command, must we in this chamber confess that we are mentally bankrupt and incapable of meeting the conditions which confront us? I do not think so. I do not believe that Canadians are less competent than other people; in some respects we are better than they; and if the time and attention of the government were seriously directed towards methods of distribution of our surplus production it would do a much greater service to the people than to adopt the attitude of taking things for granted based on the old theory of laissez faire. To-day people are demanding action. The letters I receive from various parts of the country show that the public are tired of years of masterly inactivity on the part of the government. Why can it not take some definite action other than the time-worn methods which have been tried and found wanting? In such an endeavour the government might and probably would make mistakes, but it would be far better for them to make mistakes in trying to solve the problem than to sit still, idle, and do nothing at all. I wonder what future generations will think of us. I wonder what will be their verdict upon a parliament which, when the country has hundreds of millions of bushels

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
of surplus grain, when our packing plants are full of foodstuffs, our warehouses and factories full of clothing, and yet there is so much suffering, want and distress-what will they say of a parliament which sits inactive and ineffective? I do not believe their opinion of this generation will be very high.
What the people are demanding from parliament is a measure of economic security. They are perfectly right in making that demand. It is useless for us to say that unemployment is a matter for municipalities or provincial governments; it is primarily a responsibility of the federal government, because it is through policies which we adopt that unemployment is either increased or diminished. That is not an achievement within the powers of either the municipalities or the provincial governments. The responsibility is therefore with the federal authority, and the government should assume it. In 1935 the present government pledged itself to provide economic security for the people. I do not believe anyone will contend that what the government has attempted has dealt effectively with the problem.
In many respects Canada is a fortunate country. As I have said, we have unlimited natural resources, an abundance of wealth such as few nations possess. We have also a vigorous and virile population which wants nothing but an opportunity of working those resources in order to satisfy its needs. The duty, then, rests with this government to give the people, first, the opportunity to work and develop those resources, and, second, the opportunity to so utilize them that we may have a happy and contented people.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Just before the motion is passed, I want again to underline the point of view that there is a growing dissatisfaction at the inactivity of parliament in connection with this particular matter and in general with the economic situation. This morning I happened to see a report of a speech by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer), who had some hard things to say about parliament. For example he said this:
I have come to the conclusion that Guy Fawkes was the only fellow who ever went to a parliament in the right frame of mind.
That is what the hon. member said last Friday evening at St. Thomas. I venture to say that if one of our university professors said that he would immediately be called to
book. Yet this is symptomatic of what people will accept because of the grave conditions of unemployment and general economic circumstances which confront the country. He went on to criticize on the same grounds various people connected with our public affairs. For example he said this "facetiously" -and many a thing which is in one's mind is said in truth and in jest:
Facetiously, Mr. McGeer suggested that possibly Canada had had too many bachelors at the head of her administrations. Great as he was, Right Hon. R. B. Bennett lacked something and in the speaker's opinion that was a wife and family. Sir Edward Beatty was in the same class; as for Premier W. L. Mackenzie King-"Well, I believe there is quite a lot of Conservatives in Ontario who will agree there is something lacking in Mr. King," said the speaker, amid laughter.
Then he went on:
"These old bachelors have a different outlook on life," he submitted. "Instead of looking out on unbroken trails, writing memoirs is their forte."	*
Statements of this sort are being made and accepted because, I submit, we are not grappling with the problem of unemployment and with the other conditions with which we are faced. Regarding the government Mr. McGeer had this to say:
Closing with a tribute to Premier Hepburn and his genius for getting things done through dynamic leadership, Mr. McGeer said that . . . "if he had the privilege of selecting he would sentence the Prime Minister of Canada and all members of the Canadian government to at least three terms on Mitch Hepburn's onion farm."

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, April 6, consideration in committee of Bill No. 6, to amend the Pension Act-Mr. Power-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 10-Compassionate pension or allowance.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: When this hill was last being considered by the committee, I obtained the consent of the house to consolidate Bill No. 6 with Bill No. 74, and at the suggestion of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) I agreed to have the bill reprinted. The reprints have 'been distributed to members.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Not yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: For the information of the committee I may say that all sections down to section 10 have been passed. Section 10 stood at the request of the hon. member for Vancouver South. If I remember rightly he suggested that there should be a right to appeal in connection for claims for compassionate hearing.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: My idea was that the new appeal boards should have the power to grant compassionate pensions. The discussion was along that line.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I have a report from the chairman of the pension commission. I do not think I need read it all. In 1936 I had a suggestion which I might refer to now. Under the proposed bill at that time it was suggested to set up an appeal division of the commission and to abolish the appeal court, and one of the sections of that bill provided that the appeal division might on special application in that behalf grant a pension or an allowance in any case which it considered especially meritorious. I am informed that at that time both the Canadian Legion and my hon. friend were strongly opposed-

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Don't drag me into it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Yes. My hon. friend was one of those who did not think that the appeal division should be given the right to deal with claims under the compassionate clause.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
I do not think that is
right, but if so I may have been wrong then.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I do not think it will be necessary to grant this power to the appeal board. The commission itself has made most of the awards. The appeal court made only three during the whole period of its existence. There is no reason why applications for compassionate hearing cannot be heard more than once as the condition of the applicant changes, and personally I see no reason why there should be another appeal. After all, it is a matter of the discretion of three men and the commission have used reasonable judgment up to the present. On further consideration my hon. friend will, I think, come to the conclusion that it is not absolutely necessary.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: What is the position of those cases where the crown has appealed and where the appeal has been allowed by the pension appeal court?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I do not think the crown has ever appealed, nor could it appeal on compassionate grounds.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
And what about cases
where there are meritorious circumstances? I think the commission would find it difficult to award an allowance under section 21 if there were on record a decision of the pension appeal court against the appellant.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I am informed that there has never been an appeal from the appeal court on a pension award on meritorious grounds, and that is what we are dealing with now. The crown under this legislation will have no right to appeal at all.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: As I understand the policy of the commission, they will not grant an allowance under section 21 if it is clearly contrary to other provisions in the act or contrary to a decision previously rendered. With reference to those cases where the decision of the pension appeal court has been against the appellant, would it not be difficult for the commission to consider favourably an application under section 21 when there is already on the record a decision against the applicant? Would it not be advantageous to perpetuate in this act the provisions of the existing act which give the pension appeal court the right to consider applications under section 21?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
I do not see the need for it. Section 21 is a matter entirely for the discretion of the commission. To keep on appealing in cases of discretion, going from one board to another, does not seem to me to be quite the thing to do. It did not do the soldier any good under the former legislation,

Pension Act Amendment
it is not likely to do him any good now, because it is to members of the same commission that he will appeal, although probably not the same men. I presume my hon. friend would like to have the applicant get two chances, but as I understand it he can get two chances. These requests on meritorious grounds need never be closed. If the circumstances change, and without any question of new evidence, they need never be closed. The meritorious factor is so wide that it can come up at any time. If we inserted a clause such as suggested it might give some people the idea that they should appeal, and probably cause worse heart-break, when the case is no better. Frankly, I do not think it would do any good and it might do some harm.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Is it clear that if the new appeal boards think a meritorious pension should be awarded, all they have to do in order to have that pension awarded is to refer the case to the chairman of the pension commission, who, after all, has the decision on meritorious cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: There is no reason why they should not suggest it; I think they should very properly make that suggestion.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Suppose a man made
an appeal under this clause and it was refused, when could he make another appeal if circumstances changed?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: On' meritorious grounds they can always appeal.

Section agreed to.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Is it the intention under this amendment that the widow of a pensioner who died, say in 1930, should now be able to apply for a widow's pension?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Yes, I know of several cases who have written to me since this amendment was introduced, and I was glad to be able to tell them they would benefit by it. But there will be no retroactive payments; payments will begin from the coming into force of the measure.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: It would be true also in the case of the widow of a pensioner who died in 1920?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: This bill does not come into force until July 1. Would it be possible to bring this particular section into force once the bill has been passed by the house and senate?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I hardly think so.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: It will mean a delay of two or three months to widows who would otherwise be entitled.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Give us time to get ready; we shall have quite a number of applications, then they will all be on the same footing.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Is there a provision which applies to widowed mothers of pensioners?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: This does not apply to mothers; they are looked after under an existing section. Widowed mothers are treated on an altogether different basis from widows. Generally speaking, widows who are granted pension get a pension of right, no matter what their financial condition may be, and they all get the same amount, namely $60 a month; whereas the widowed mother's case is in the discretion of the commission provided there was what is called prospective dependency, and provided also she is in need. There are certain restrictions with regard to earnings of unmarried members of the family. But that is treated in another section, No. 33.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I wanted to find out if this would apply to the widowed mother if the pensioner died of something that was not attributable to his war disabilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Do I understand this section is retroactive with respect to entitlement?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: But not with respect to payment?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Would the minister give
consideration to a provision to give the pension commission discretion to allow payments to be continued to the widow of a pensioner who, under the act at present would otherwise not be entitled to pension, for a period of, say a year, as is done under the War Veterans' Allowance Act. Since this bill was up last time I have checked up on the proceedings O; the last Canadian Legion convention at Fort William, in January and February, 1938, and one of their resolutions was:
That this convention reaffirm that the Pension Act be amended permitting pension paid at the time of death to be continued to the widow for at least one year and where the amount is less than that allowed under the War Veterans' Allowance Act that it be increased to that amount.
Pension Act Amendment

The maximum under that act is, I believe, $40 a month. Time and again we run into eases of great hardship because widows are cut right off at the time of the husband's death. Would it not be possible to have an amendment that would meet the suggestion of the Canadian Legion?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I have given that a great deal of consideration for many years and I cannot agree with my hon. friend. If there is really a meritorious claim the pension commission has discretion to award pension.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Could the pension commission award pension to a widow who would not qualify under the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Why not? Under section 21.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
I brought this question up before, but I do not think I said anything particular about it at that time. Perhaps the minister can enlighten me if I ask my question again now.
It relates to the case of. a widow with several children, I believe five or six, of a returned soldier who was pensioned, who, while he was in Christie street hospital, had fainted and fallen, or at any rate had fallen on the floor as a result of his war disability and who also fell on the street on several occasions. About a year ago he obtained a position in a camp in northern Ontario. During the winter he was laid off or decided to go home to Toronto, and on his trip from the camp to the railway station he died. The coroner up countiy, who may have been thoroughly qualified, and probably was, made an investigation and reported on the death paper that the man died from pneumonia. That having been once written on the death paper, the widow apparently had no claim, on account of pneumonia not being a war disability. But on numerous occasions this man had fallen as a result of bis war disability, and it is alleged that on this occasion on the way from the station he fell and was frozen to death before he could get up. That widow apparently has no redress; the coroner's word overrides everything. The man was dead when he was found; the body had been frozen perhaps twenty-four hours; it would be a day or two before the coroner would get it, and doubtless the coroner did not know that this man had been subject to fainting spells as a result of his war disability. I have had the case up two or three times with the pension board, but so far the coroner's statement is taken above all other evidence of the hospital attendants and other persons who knew this man to be subject to fainting by reason of his war disability. I shall be glad if this poor widow will qualify under this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I do not know whether or not she will qualify; that depends entirely on the pension commission. There are thousands of pensions that I might grant if I had the right to do so, but parliament will not give me that right. If my hon. friend will give me the right to grant pensions I shall have pleasure in granting his request any time he asks me to do so.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I would be inclined to take the minister's wish ahead of the statement of some coroner who may not have known anything about the man's previous condition.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend pleaded this case before the pension commission, and apparently the pension commission could not see its way clear to grant a pension, so I cannot do it. The law precludes me from granting a pension.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Does the statement of a coroner go ahead of the statement of the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I do not know anything about that, but my hon. friend said he had placed his case before the pension commission, which under the law has full power, authority and exclusive jurisdiction in such matters. If the pension commission say they cannot grant a pension I cannot do it; parliament cannot do it; the Prime Minister cannot do it, and even His Excellency the Governor General cannot do it. .

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Would not this woman qualify under this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: She would always have a claim if her husband died as a result of his war service. In the second place, if he did not die as a result of war service and the case is specially meritorious the commission may grant a pension. Apparently they have not seen fit to do so, and there is nothing I can do about the matter. There is nothing my hon. friend can do and nothing parliament can do until they change the law and give the minister the right to grant pensions if he so desires.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
I wish to be clear on this point. A moment ago the minister told the hon. member for Vancouver South that the commission had power to grant an allowance in specially meritorious cases. I am anxious to be clear as to how that power may be exercised, because in making representations to the commission on behalf of pensioners I have always understood that it was not possible to exercise that discretion if it were contrary to the intention of the act; that is, if other sections prohibited the payment of a

Pension Act Amendment
pension, it would not be possible. I have in mind the case of a man who had meritorious service overseas. He was seconded to the imperial forces as an officer and established entitlement on account of chronic asthma and bronchitis. By order of the authorities he was admitted to the hospital and an operation was performed under a general anaesthetic. The evidence was that as a result of that anaesthetic he succumbed to a form of pneumonia. I have here a copy of the final decision of the pension appeal court. There are many meritorious circumstances surrounding this particular case, but I understand the obstacle to action under the meritorious clause would be this decision of the appeal court expressly ruling against the application for pension, that it would be contrary to the policy of the commission to grant a meritorious allowance in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that I cannot tell him just what was in the minds of either the members of the appeal court or the members of the commission in interpreting section 21. If he will cast his mind back to 1923 or 1924, when section 21 was inserted in the act, when, if I remember rightly my hon. friend acted as counsel for the Great War Veterans' Association, he will remember that at that time the committee wished to give the commission some discretion in awarding pensions where they were barred by the statute. I think I had something to do with drafting section 21, and I have always had in mind that the section was intended to cover cases in which the commission could not under the statute grant a pension. It was rather for that purpose than for the purpose for which it has been used in later years; that is, in cases where there was no evidence of fact. It was intended to cover cases which were barred by statute rather than cases which were barred by fact. That was always my understanding of the value of section 21, and I think my hon. friend will agree that this was in the mind of the committee which brought down that legislation. I am also under the impression that in most cases the commission at any rate have taken that view, that it would apply to a person who had meritorious service but who was otherwise barred by the statute. I do not think there is any doubt at all about that. There is no doubt in my mind as to what was intended, just as there is no doubt as to the interpretation placed upon this section, although that may not have been followed in all cases.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps the best test would be how many pensions under the meritorious section were granted to widows during the last fiscal year.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I have not that information at hand, but more have been granted in the last two or three years than were ever granted before.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES

speechtext: Hon. J. G. GARDINER moved the second reading of Bill No. 88, to encourage the improvement of cheese and cheese factories.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understood that the minister was going to make an explanation.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill is to promote the welfare of the cheese industry. As members of the house [DOT] are aware, there has been some difficulty in the dairy industry in Canada on account of the fact that there has been, during the past year particularly, an overproduction of butter in relation to its consumption in Canada. It has been found by long experience that it is difficult to export Canadian butter and sell it in competition, say with New Zealand butter, in the British market, partly because their costs of production are not as high as ours in Canada where we have different climatic conditions. There has, therefore, been an effort to keep our production within Canada related to our consumption. That effort was interfered with somewhat by an export of butter from Canada to the old country in the fall of 1937, which left a shortage of butter supply in this country amounting to about five or six million pounds in the early part of 1938. That shortage of supply in Canada resulted in an increase in price, which eventually brought more butter fat into the production of butter and less into the production of cheese in proportion to the amount supplied. An effort has been made this year to reverse that process and to encourage the putting of more butter fat into the production of cheese, and this bill is brought before the house for the purpose of promoting that end. In order to promote it we are doing three different things.
In the first place we are paying a premium upon high grade cheese. The bill as it was introduced in the house will require amendment. It was our intention that there should
Dairying Industry-Cheese

be a premium of one cent a pound paid on cheese that scores 93, and a premium of two cents a pound on cheese that scores 94. Approximately two per cent of our cheese scores 94, which is the highest score; and 33.75 per cent of our cheese scores 93; so that, in all, somewhere between 35 and 36 per cent of our cheese will this year score 93 or 94. The greater part of the remainder scores 92. I think about 8 per cent would be under 92, and the rest is in the 92 classification. Our objective is to try to raise that lower grade cheese to the 93 level by paying a premium of one cent a pound on cheese that scores 93 and two cents a pound on cheese that scores 94.
The greater part of the cheese produced in Canada and entering into export is produced in Ontario and Quebec. Considerable encouragement has been given in Ontario to the building of better curing rooms and to the improvement of plants. Considerable encouragement has been given in the province of Quebec also, but up to date there has probably been more done along that line in Ontario than in Quebec. Ontario is producing a larger proportion of cheese that scores 93 than in Quebec. So in this bill we are making provision to encourage those who are operating cheese factories to improve their equipment. We are offering an encouragement of 50 per cent of the cost of improving curing rooms and 50 per cent of the cost of putting in new equipment, particularly the type of equipment that has the hoop form, which makes cheese of a type and size suitable to the export trade. We are setting aside approximately one-quarter of a million dollars for the purpose of encouraging this improvement in equipment and in curing rooms, and for the purpose of encouraging the amalgamation of some of the smaller plants, where in a district there will be sometimes two or three, into one plant. We hope that by spending approximately one-quarter of a million dollars during the present year to make it possible for many of those who are to-day producing cheese that scores 92, to produce next year, if not in the latter part of this year, cheese that scores 93.
We are giving that encouragement at this time to the industry in those areas where the condition that I have outlined exists, and we hope that with these two methods of encouragement we shall be able to place a much larger percentage of our high grade cheese in the British market and also to keep the price of cheese at a point where there is an advantage in the production of cheese over the production of butter, and thus retain a greater percentage of butter fat in the

cheese industry rather than have it go into the production of butter. In that way we shall assist both the butter and the cheese industries.

As far as I can gather from
his remarks the minister has been attempting to prove that the bonus of 1J cents on cheese instituted in 1935 did not have the effect of increasing production, and he points to the 1935 figures which, he says, showed an increase of only a million pounds. But the minister knows, as everyone does, that cheese production is commenced in the spring; the cheese factories open in the spring and carry on during the summer months. The bonus that year did not become effective until July, when it was impossible for butter makers to change their production to cheese. The next spring, however, since there was a small surplus left in this bonus account and some prospect of getting the government to continue the grant, there was an increase in the number of cheese factories, with the result that cheese production increased in that year by 19,000,000 pounds.
The minister states that there has been a great increase in our exports of cheese to the United States. That was due more or less to a temporary condition. I do not think he or anyone else would seriously argue that we can continue to export cheese to the United States against a five cent duty, which, I understand, is in force at the present time. Our natural market for cheese is in Great Britain, where it always has been; and I agree with the minister that everything possible should be done to preserve that market.
While I am on my feet I want to make just one suggestion in regard to this grant of 50 per cent of certain expenditures to cheese factories which may unite. I do not understand why a grant should be made to two small factories that may unite in order to improve existing buildings or construct new ones, while a much larger factory that may produce more than the two smaller ones together is not given any grant at all. It seems to me that if this grant is being made to enable factories to insulate and fix up their storerooms in order that cheese may be stored under better conditions, the grant should be made to larger factories as well if they wish to improve their refrigeration. One of the most important factors in connection with the production of cheese is the storage for the first two or three weeks after production. If the cheese is kept too warm it deteriorates rapidly, so that refrigeration is very necessary indeed not only for the first two or three weeks but for an even longer time. Therefore

Dairying Industry-Cheese
I think it would be a good thing if we could make some provision whereby we could age our cheese for three or six months, or perhaps even a year; I think it would be one of the best things we could do in order to improve the price obtained for our cheese in the old country. I should like the minister to explain why this grant is made available to two small factories that may unite, while it is not made available to much larger factories.
