speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the daily industry will thoroughly appreciate the assistance that is being offered by the government in giving a premium- I should not like to call it a bonus-to encourage the manufacture of cheese in Canada. I think if we go back over the history of Canadian cheese production to find what has probably decided the government to come to the conclusion to offer this premium, we shall probably feel entitled to ask that the premium be paid not only on cheese that scores 94 and 93 but also on cheese that scores 92.
We cannot consider the problem solely in terms of cheese, because the idea of giving a bonus on cheese is to dispose of the milk which now creates a surplus of butter on the home market. When there is a surplus of butter, it gluts our local market, and consequently the domestic price falls all the time to lower and lower levels. In 1936, which was about an average year, the production of creamery butter was 250,000,000 pounds, and of dairy butter, 114,000,000 pounds, or a total of about 365,000000 pounds. In Canada we consume about 1,000,000 pounds of butter daily, and have done so for the past few years. We cannot easily export a surplus of butter because there is too much humidity and probably not quite enough salt in it; in other words, it is not quite hard enough, and there is no real demand for it. When we do export some, it is not of a quality which compares favourably with the product of other exporting countries. Therefore we are not in a position readily to face the competition of butter exporters elsewhere. We can, however,

face competition in cheese, and I can easily understand the reason why the minister is offering a premium on the manufacture of cheese. While manufacturing the necessary amount of butter for domestic consumption, we should have no surplus, but the excess of milk should be diverted into the manufacture of cheese, for which we have a practically unlimited market.
In 1937 we manufactured 246,000,000 pounds of creamery butter and 113,000,000 pounds of dairy butter, or, in all, 360,000,000 pounds. That year we were short to the extent of
5.000.	000 pounds. Consequently the price of butter in Canada was high, or if not high, at least satisfactory to the producer. The shortage caused the importation of about
5.000.	000 pounds of butter in January, February and part of March, 1938.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: That was a mistake too.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
Well, it may have been a mistake; the hon. member for Haldimand seems to think so; but if he wants to follow the ordinary course of trade he will find that, with only 360,000,000 pounds of butter manufactured in Canada and a possible consumption of 365,000,000 pounds it was to the advantage of the consumer as well as of the trade to import some butter in order to supply distributors who were short. At any rate, 5,000,000 pounds were imported early in 1938, and in March of that year the wholesale price went up to thirty-five cents. What did that do? It encouraged dairymen to go into the manufacture of butter to a far larger extent than should have been the case, with the result that in 1938 we manufactured 267,000,000 pounds of creamery butter and also- the figures are not available from the bureau of statistics, but I have secured the information from rather good authority-about 120,000,000 pounds of dairy butter. As a result we were left with a surplus of over 25,000,000 pounds at the end of the year. It was very difficult to dispose of that butter in outside markets, and the price this year has fallen to new lows. To make my remarks more brief. I may point out that at the present time butter fat is worth about 20 to 21J cents a pound, or the equivalent of 21 to 22 cents a pound of butter. About the same situation existed in the years 1932 and 1933. What it means is that during the coming year butter prices will again be down to 16 and 17 cents a pound, which is below the cost of production, and the farmers, particularly those in the dairy industry, will be in a very difficult situation.
If the premium the Minister of Agriculture is offering at the present time were extended

Dairying Industry-Cheese
to include 92 cheese, I am sure that the problem would solve itself. Instead of sending their milk to be turned into butter, people would convert it into cheese, but it must be made worth their while. At the present time cheese is worth 10i or lOf cents a pound, and I should like to explain, for the information of those who are not familiar with the matter, what that means. On an average production for the whole year, 100 pounds of milk will produce 9J pounds of cheese. In 1932 cheese sold at an average of 9-74 cents; in 1933 the average was 10-11 cents. Let us accept a figure of 10 cents, because there are many indications that conditions will be much the same as they were in 1932 and 1933. Nine and a quarter pounds of cheese sold at 10 cents will give the producer a return of 92| cents. Deduct the cost of fabrication, which is two cents a pound, or 9i pounds at two cents, that is 18A cents, and you have 74 cents net per 100 pounds of milk. There is not a farmer in Canada who can produce 100 pounds of milk for 74 cents.
Last year an investigation, conducted on 780 farms throughout the dominion, was made by the economics branch of the Department of Agriculture. I will not give the figures which were arrived at with reference to the various operations, because we are talking in terms of cheese; I shall simply take the cost of production of milk in a cheese zone, selecting for that purpose the zone of Ottawa. It was shown that the cost of producing 100 pounds of milk for the manufacture of cheese was $1.24. In 1933, when conditions were similar to those prevailing this year, a milk investigation was carried on by a committee of this house. After a thorough and careful inquiry it was ascertained that milk for the same purpose was costing the producer $1.28 per 100 pounds. So that surely it will be very difficult to interest the producer of milk in the fabrication of cheese when he knows that the cost of his milk is from SI .24 to $1.28, and that his return is going to be somewhere about 74 cents per 100 pounds. There is a deficit of 50 cents per hundred.
It may be said that the situation is probably just as bad in connection with the production of butter, but that is not quite the case. If the producer is paid about the same price for butter fat he still has the skim milk which he can use to feed small animals and chickens, and for other purposes. Skim milk has been shown to be worth fifteen cents more than the by-product known as whey in the manufacturing of cheese. It is fifteen cents per 100 pounds more to the farmer who produces butter, of about five cents per pound
of butter fat. Consequently, if you wish to place those who are producing cheese on the same footing as those who are producing butter, selling their milk at the same price per pound of butter fat, they must have a better price per pound of butter fat in the manufacture of cheese than in the production of butter because they will always be inclined to go back to butter for the reason I have just given, that at least they have the skim milk which they can feed to young animals such as pigs and calves, and to chickens. They get some revenue from that skim milk and they make a profit from it. Therefore, if the legislation now before us is intended to divert the surplus of milk that is glutting the market with butter, destroying the domestic price, the premium must be of necessity not only on cheese grading 93 and 94, but on cheese grading 92, 93 and 94. These are of good quality and no one will criticize the quality of this cheese. I say, therefore, that if you want to interest those engaged in the dairy industiy and to induce them to send their milk for the production of cheese, provided they produce No. 1, they should be given greater encouragement.
I do not know what words I could use that would be strong enough to convey my views with regard to this amendment to section 8 of this bill. After all, the one cent on 93 cheese is only one cent on 33-7 per cent of the production of cheese. If you tell me that you are anxious to interest people in greater production of an article and that you are going to give them a premium on only 33-7 per cent of production of first quality, I suggest that you will not convince anyone that there is much encouragement there. And the two cents, mind you, is offered on only T9 per cent of the production of cheese; consequently two cents a pound on less than 2 per cent of the production of a commodity is on such a small proportion of the whole production that it will be positively unattractive to those engaged in the industry.
If the one cent were paid on 92 cheese, which is 53-3 per cent of production, or
672.000	pounds of what was produced last year, and two cents on the other grades, rep-' resenting 400,000 pounds, it would take $S00,-000 for the two cent premium on 93 and 94, and the one cent premium on 92, representing
672.000	pounds, would be $1,472,000. In my humble judgment this would constitute a serious attempt to induce the farmers to divert into the manufacture of cheese the surplus of milk now going into butter, and this cheese could easily be sold in the markets which we now enjoy and are pretty sure to enjoy in the future. Undoubtedly it would

help the situation if those engaged in the dairy industry took steps to see that no district should produce more than a given quantity of butter, because if they do, they will destroy their own market. If this is not done, the present unsatisfactory condition will continue. From 1930 to 1939 the farmers have passed through some serious times, and we have witnessed some of the gravest crises the world has seen. I am not blaming any political party; the subject is too important for playing politics. Really, the only good year the industry has had since 1930 was 1937. That year the industry did well, but from 1930 to 1934 inclusive the farmers went backwards all the time. We had to pass legislation to help them in every way, by means of a moratorium, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and in other ways. The young people could not be interested to stay on the farms. Matters rather improved in 1937. In 1938 the price was fair, but in 1939 the people are not in a position to cope with the odds against them. They cannot face many more years of the distress and the difficulties that they have had to put up with. There will occur many more bankruptcies in the dairy industry in the year to come than have taken place in several years past, because the farmers are not sufficiently strong financially to face the music much longer. They are just holding on. If in the coming year they are to receive 74 cents per 100 pounds of milk while it costs them SI.20 to produce it, it can readily be seen that they cannot continue in the industry. This is one of the most urgent matters for the government to deal with.
I am not going to refer for the moment to the fact that there were urgent problems in other parts of the country and that they were dealt with in order to try to save agriculture there, any more than simply to say we claim that the dairy industry in the east is facing one of the most urgent problems that it has ever faced in all its history, and that the government will be well advised to spend $1,500,000 during this year in order to try to help that industry. I repeat that I hope it will have the effect of bringing the output of butter again within the consumption of the domestic market only as well as giving a better return for the, cheese. I am in accord with most of the provisions of this bill. The amendment now under discussion is to give two cents a pound bonus on 94 and one cent on 93, and we have had the suggestion by the hon. member who has just spoken to extend that and pay one cent on cheese scoring 92. To my mind there is a distinct difference between a premium paid for quality and a bonus. If we apply that one cent to 92 grade cheese we pass the stage of a premium and enter upon the principle of a bonus. In fairness to the butter producers I am not sure that I could support that principle, because we would then be paying a direct bonus upon at least 90 to 93 per cent of the entire cheese production of Ontario; it certainly would be a bonus, not a premium.
By paying a premium for quality and so improving the quality of the cheese and increasing the amount exported and the price received for it, you may recompense the country for the amount taken from the treasury to pay that premium. To my mind that justifies the principle of paying a premium for quality cheese. We must remember that we have a large quantity of milk entering the production of milk powder in Canada. This matter that we are discussing does not of course affect to a very great extent milk entering the powder plants, but I believe we have in Canada to-day a large surplus of milk powder, and we shall have a reduction in the quantity of milk entering into the production of this commodity this year. There is a strong possibility that the payment of this premium will divert a quantity of milk from the creameries to the cheese factories, and that should be of assistance to

the butter producer by reducing the production of butter. But representing a constituency where there is one cheese factory and very many creameries, I think we must bear in mind that the butter producer is operating under extreme difficulties. It has been mentioned that skim milk is worth fifteen cents per 100 pounds more than whey, but we should bear in mind that there is less work on the farm in preparing milk to be sent to the cheese factory than in preparing cream to send it to a creamery, because for that you must have a separator, must wash the separator, so a certain amount of that fifteen cents must be credited to the additional work which is necessary in order to produce that skim milk.
I see no reason why I could not support the principle of paying the premium of two cents for cheese scoring 94 and one cent for cheese scoring 93, but I would hesitate to endorse the principle of turning right back to a direct bonus and departing from the principle of a premium for a quality product.

My understanding is that the method followed in Ontario and Quebec and in most instances where cheese is made is the paying of a commission to the factory for making the cheese, then the cheese is sold and the amount received for it is distributed to the producers. Of course this amount will be paid to the cheese factory, will become a part of the price for which the cheese is disposed of and will be distributed to the producer by that method, so that all the premium paid will go to the producer of the cheese.
With regard to the question raised by the hon. member for Prescott and very well answered in part by the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, I should like to say that the intention of this legislation is to pay a premium in order to improve the quality. We believe that an improvement in quality will have the result of increasing the sale and
bringing about a better price for the commodity over a period of years. With that idea in mind our desire, of course, is to satisfy our best market for cheese, namely the United Kingdom. My understanding is that about 60 per cent of all the cheese which now goes to the United Kingdom market is held for maturing, and because that is so, that is what really gives our cheese its reputation in Great Britain. Our desire, of course, is to raise that percentage much higher than 60 per cent. One reason why it is important that this should be done is the fact that most of our cheese which goes to the United Kingdom is exported during a period when it is not yet suited to that market, and in most instances that cheese will be kept in store in the old country for from nine to ten months and, in many instances, from fifteen to eighteen months. So only the top score cheese will remain in storage for that length of time and be reasonably certain still to measure up to the tests it passed when it was put in store for curing.
So if we are to retain that market and keep our cheese at the high standard that we hope to attain, we must send over there the best quality that we can obtain. Therefore we believe it is worth while to pay a premium to those who produce that cheese, in order to place it upon that market in that condition.
Not only is it important that we should have good cheese on the British market; it is also most important that we should have good cheese for our own market. the prices are low, and while the March price this year is low compared with March during the years we have just come through, it was low during those years as well, as a rule. It is not an indication of what the price is going to be when we get further into the season.
I might add that there is, of course, the possibility of overdoing even the matter of paying a premium. We have at the moment a market which is fairly well developed for a certain commodity, and particularly for certain amounts and certain grades of the commodity, but we have not an unlimited market. It should be remembered that back in 1907 we were exporting to the old land, if I remember the figures well over
200,000,000 pounds, and at that time New Zealand was exporting about 27,000,000 pounds. In very recent years we have been exporting in the neighbourhood of 53,000,000 pounds when New Zealand was exporting to Great Britain 190,000,000 pounds. In other words, we have allowed New Zealand over a period of years from 1900 down to the last two or three years to take possession of the British market with a lower grade cheese which was selling under ours to the extent of li to 3 cents a pound. But they are in that market, and when we try now to reenter it, of course we have to an extent to take away the market from others who have occupied it during the years we did not occupy it. I think we have done fairly well in getting back three years ago to the extent of 19 per cent, and raising that in the succeeding year to 27 or 28 per cent over previous years. This last year we have dropped a little; but if you follow the history of either the reductions or the increases in our sales of cheese in the old country you will find that periodically we rise for a short time, then we may drop down, and then we come back again. We went down in exactly the same way. We would go down over a period of years, then we would rise again for a year or two, and then we would go back again. At the present time we are on the up-grade, and I want to do something which is fairly sound in the matter of cheese production, and keep possession of the markets available. If we overdo it we shall injure our business rather than help it. We feel that we are giving the inducement which is necessary this year in order to keep the production in step with the market which is available, and we hope that through promotion we shall be able to raise our market even higher in succeeding years.

speechtext:
Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 84, to amend the Dairy Industry Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 1-Advisory committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The minister stated the other night that this advisory board had been asked for by certain organizations. Who are they?

Dairy Industry Act-Advisory Committee

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The national dairy
council.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Will the members of the board be paid for their services out of the federal treasury?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: No salary is provided, but we will pay the travelling expenses when we call them to meetings.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Generally, what are their
duties?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: We had a considerable discussion last fall when it was anticipated we would have a greater amount of butter in storage than we could take care of in the local market this year, and different suggestions were made as to ways and means of dealing with that over-supply. Some people thought we should set up a board to take possession and try to dispose of it. We did not see any practical way of carrying that out, and after a good deal of discussion we agreed that it would be a good thing to have an advisory committee that would keep in close contact with the officials of the department who gather statistics and information from time to time as regards dairy production. This committee would act in an advisory capacity as between the producers and the trade and the government, and also as between the department and the trade itself, taking the matter into consideration earlier in the season than we did last year, thereby trying to avoid overproduction of either commodity, and also assisting in every way possible in getting transfers of milk or butter fat from one to the other at an earlier stage in the season.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: We have such an advisory committee on seeds. They have certain duties such as setting up standards and grades from year to year. This committee will not have anything of that kind to do.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: No; their duties will consist in what I have outlined. They will try to keep in closer contact with the department and those who are producing, and with the trade, with a view to keeping people instructed as to necessities.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I gather from what the minister says about the duties of the committee that they are to act in an advisory capacity with regard to surpluses of butter that may be on the market. Perhaps the minister will take this opportunity to inform the committee what is being done about the surplus butter which the government intends to buy for distribution throughout the country in order to take the surplus off the market.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The government is not doing what I have seen suggested in the newspapers. The government is not buying butter directly, taking it out of storage and shipping it here and there throughout the country. We have approached the Red Cross and have made almost complete arrangements with them to take charge of any distribution which is made. We are issuing vouchers which are good for No. 1 butter, and they will be distributed under direction of the Red Cross to relief and charitable organizations where persons are not now obtaining as much butter as they might use. These vouchers will be presented to any merchant who is selling butter and are good for so many pounds of No. 1 butter. It is thought, of course, that, if that practice is followed, the customer will take only No. 1 butter, and while some of that butter will come out of storage, a considerable part of the butter in storage last year is not No. 1, so that much of this butter may be used as it is produced and sold into the trade. Some of it may come out of storage, but the butter will be purchased from the merchant by the individual in the ordinary manner. As vouchers are presented to the merchant they will accumulate; at the end of the month they will be presented to the bank; the bank will redeem them, and they will come back to the government through that source. The government will have paid the price of the butter at that particular time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I thank the minister for his explanation. I thought the distribution would be made pretty much in that way. Butter is being already distributed, however, to needy people through these organizations, and I do not think the minister would suggest that the people now on relief have not been getting their full quota. If that were the situation, it would be rather a reflection on the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and on the activities of the different bodies to which his estimates go. I do not, however, intend to discuss the matter further to-night. May I ask how many members will be on this board and who will appoint them? Will the national dairy council and the other organizations or the producers have an opportunity of appointing some of the members, or will they all be nominated by the governor in council?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Under the bill they are to be appointed by the minister, but in actual practice we will consult with the organization recommended and with other organizations concerned.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
How many?
3136	COMMONS
Dairy Industry Act-Advisory Committee

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONSTITUTION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There will probably be five or seven. I do not know whether it will be necessary to have one from each province

probably not. We will divide Canada into different sections and get one from each of the different sections where production is heavy. As regards relief consumption of butter, I would only say this. I do not know whether my hon. friend has had the experience of living in a home where they have difficulty in securing the necessary foodstuffs. If he has, he will probably find that the first thing the mother gets along without is butter. When she is not able to get butter she often gets a cheap jam or something of that kind, and when she cannot get that she just does without. There are many homes in which the mother and father are perhaps too proud to go on what we generally call relief, and they get along for months, sometimes years, without any butter at all. The only organizations that get in touch with homes like that are the Salvation Army and the charitable organizations of the churches, welfare organizations, and organizations like the Red Cross. These organizations come in contact with these people often in spite of the people themselves, and find that the children are going without butter. If butter is supplied to them these homes can use it to good advantage to the extent of about six pounds in two weeks for a family of five. That would be about the normal consumption. On the other hand, while it would not be proper to say that relief organizations are not giving the absolutely necessary requirements of butter, they are, generally speaking, giving only about half the above amount, and one could double the consumption of butter in those homes without any more being consumed than in the average home where people buy all the butter they want. So there is considerable room for extending the consumption of butter, first in homes where none is being used now by people who are not necessarily on relief but are getting a little assistance from charitable organizations, and second, in the families on relief lists. By encouraging greater consumption of butter in those homes we hope to dispose of three or four million pounds.

I notice under this vote
there is apparently an increase in staff of twenty-one. Why is that?

speechtext:
No, there is a total decrease
of seven.
What work is done by this bureau?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: This is a bureau provided at government expense to prepare and plead cases of applicants for pension. The soldier is not obliged to retain a solicitor; when he thinks he has a claim for pension he goes to the veterans' bureau which prepares his case fully and pleads it before the pension bodies.
Is the proportion of soldiers who take advantage of the services of the bureau increasing or decreasing?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The proportion is well over 90 per cent. There are very few cases now in which the applicants engage the services of outside solicitors; and when they do, almost invariably the veterans' bureau assists the

Suppy-Pensions
solicitor. I know of very few within the last year. I think the veterans' bureau has been doing good work, satisfactory to the soldiers.

Item agreed to.
Pensions branch-Services to veterans and dependents.
2S9. Sheltered employment, $72,590.

Will the minister explain
this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: This provides for the accommodation, equipment and other expenses in providing sheltered employment for returned soldiers in vetcraft shops, and cost of transportation for blinded or totally disabled pensioners requiring the service of an escort. That was granted as a result of recommendations of the parliamentary committee some years ago. Also payments to Canadian National Institute for the Blind for training of and services rendered to blinded soldiers; also payments to the Red Cross for 75 per cent of the operating loss on the factory in Victoria and salaries of trade instructors in vetcraft shops and wages of operatives.
How many men are employed in the vetcraft shops; how many shops are there, and where are they located?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The number employed as of December 31, 1938 was: in Toronto factory, 55; in Montreal factory, 45, and at the Red Cross workshop in Victoria, 25; a total of 125.
Wages paid in departmental workshops from April 1 to December 31, 1938, $60,649.07. Wages paid from commencement of operations to December 31, 1938, $1,655,480.75.
Are all the wages paid out of this vote, or are part of the funds raised from other sources?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They are all paid out of this vote. A considerable amount of money comes into the vetcraft shops under this item. All the poppies and wreath emblems sold to the Canadian Legion for distribution are made under this, and the money is returned to the consolidated revenue fund, so that really while we do not quite make a profit we pretty well break even.
Then is the situation really that this $72,000 odd is required to balance the account?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
We have a turn-over account of $250,000 in a year, and the factories could not operate without this capital. Some time in January, as a rule, when the reports are all in from the poppy fund sales on Armistice day we get a cheque for $50,000 or $60,000 from the Canadian Legion, depending on sales,
and then, of course, there are the sales of the other products of the vetcraft shops, such as tables, chairs and so on.

Is the output confined to
poppies?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No; they make tables, chairs, bookcases and quite a line of articles that are usually sold through the department stores.
I was going to ask the value of this output last year, for instance?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: About $250,000 tum-over.
Is there any advertising of the products?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We have salesmen travelling throughout Ontario and Quebec. At present I think the sales are largely confined to the larger department stores; I know Eatons and Simpsons take quite a proportion of our production. At one time we had a traveller going round northern Ontario and the outlying districts; in fact, he still has his customers there.
Would it not be possible to make room for more veterans in the shops if some advertising were done?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am afraid not. That matter has been discussed a number of times; we run into the question of competition with ordinary industrial firms and the business is not profitable. It costs us about $30 a month per man, really, because the men are disabled to some extent and do not do as good work perhaps as the labourer in a factory. We have already closed six shops during the course of the last eight years.
Was that because there was no demand for these products?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It was simply because we were keeping the men in these shops; they were disabled and they had a steady job and were costing the country something like $25 or $30 a month. They would not graduate from the shops. The original idea was that there should be some labour tum-over, but now, particularly in Toronto and Montreal, we seem to be in the business and it is not very easy to get out of it. We have a number of men whom we cannot very well turn out on the street, so we are in it and I suppose we will stay in it for some little time to come.
What provision was made for the men in the shops that were closed?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The number of men in
those shops had shrunk very much. The shop in Hamilton had only about twelve men. and the shop in Halifax eight or nine, so
Suppy-Pensions

really it was not worth while keeping them on. We simply closed up the shops, after giving the men ample notice.
Were these men simply turned out on the street?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They were all pensioners.
It struck me that this was a commendable way of looking after some of these disabled men.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We have gone into workshops also in Montreal, as my hon. friend knows, with the object of getting some kind of a labour turn-over. We have established workshops which are not quite the same thing as these vetcraft shops. There is no overlapping, but they are carrying on somewhat similar work in the hope of training or, I should say, reconditioning the men so that they may obtain ordinary positions in the industrial field. We were extremely successful for a while, although perhaps we are not so successful at the moment.
The average age would be going up now.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes; the average age would be going up, and it is not a very easy thing to take a man fifty years of age and at the and of three months certify that he is fit to go into a factory or be a carpenter or undertake ironworking and things of that kind.
Why could we not use these shops for training younger men, that is, men in their early forties?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We cannot get the old employees into other shops; that is the best reason. If my hon. friend could get these men placed elsewhere, I should be glad to try some others, but they like to work for the government.
Could you not expand your plants in order to provide room for some of the younger men? You see, there are other votes here that are supposed to help provide work for these unemployed veterans.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not imagine that we could compete with ordinary industrial concerns. The results would not be commensurate with the expenditure involved in establishing large government factories to do the kind of work that we are doing at the present time.
